madrid-01.ev: Nationalist columns break into University City and meet Republican defenders fighting building by building.

q.t: Which building became a Nationalist bastion in the University City?
q.x: The Hospital Clínico became a Nationalist bastion while the Faculty of Philosophy was a Republican strongpoint. The line then froze until March 1939.

madrid-01.rem: This salient marks the closest Franco's army came to taking Madrid by storm; the front here stayed frozen for over two years.
madrid-01.st: In mid-November 1936 Nationalist columns under Varela and Asensio, led by Moroccan Regulares and the Legion, crossed the Manzanares into the half-built University City. The XI and XII International Brigades and the Durruti column fought them building by building; Durruti was mortally wounded here, though how he was shot is still debated. The line then froze until Madrid surrendered in March 1939. Today the rebuilt campus shows a few repaired façades and a 2011 International Brigades memorial.

madrid-02.ev: Colonel Moscardó holds the Alcázar through a 70-day Republican siege until Varela's troops relieve it.

q.t: Who relieved the besieged Alcázar on 27 September 1936?
q.x: Franco diverted his march on Madrid, and Varela's Army of Africa relieved the fortress on 27 September. Killings in the town followed the capture of Toledo.

madrid-02.rem: The siege became the founding legend of Francoism; the famous telephone call between Moscardó and his son is questioned by historians.
madrid-02.st: When the coup failed in Toledo, Colonel José Moscardó shut himself in the Alcázar with Civil Guards, cadets, Falangists, their families and left-wing hostages, whose fate is unclear. Republican militias besieged and mined it for 70 days until Varela's Army of Africa relieved it on 27 September 1936; killings in the town followed. The siege became the founding legend of Francoism. Today the rebuilt Alcázar houses the Army Museum, with Moscardó's office preserved and models of the siege.

madrid-03.ev: The British Battalion holds this knoll for about seven hours against Nationalist attack.

q.t: Which unit was thrown onto Suicide Hill on 12 February 1937?
o: The British Battalion of the XV International Brigade
q.x: The British Battalion of the XV International Brigade held the knoll for about seven hours; the line bent but held.

madrid-03.rem: The writer Christopher Caudwell was among those who died on this hill; the Jarama front froze here until 1939.
madrid-03.st: On 12 February 1937, during the Nationalist offensive to cut the Madrid–Valencia road, the British Battalion of the XV International Brigade was sent onto this knoll above the Jarama. For about seven hours it held against Regulares and Legionaries backed by artillery, and only a fraction of its men still stood at nightfall; the writer Christopher Caudwell was among the dead. The line bent but held. Today a stone cairn and plaques stand on the open hilltop.

madrid-04.ev: Pingarrón hill changes hands in hand-to-hand fighting; the Lincoln Battalion attacks it on 27 February.

q.t: What support was the Lincoln Battalion promised but denied on 27 February?
q.x: The Americans under Robert Merriman were ordered to attack without the promised artillery and air support and lost well over half their men.

madrid-04.rem: The Nationalists kept the hill, and the battle ended in stalemate with both armies dug in until 1939.
madrid-04.st: Pingarrón dominated the Jarama battlefield and changed hands several times in hand-to-hand fighting. Nationalist troops took it in mid-February 1937, and Republican units including Líster's men and the XV International Brigade tried repeatedly to retake it. On 27 February the Abraham Lincoln Battalion under Robert Merriman attacked without promised artillery and air support and suffered very heavy losses, the Irish poet Charles Donnelly among the dead. Today ridge-top trenches and stone parapets overlook the Jarama valley.

madrid-05.ev: Franco's basilica and cross are cut into the Guadarrama granite, partly by political prisoners.
madrid-05.rem: Dead of both sides lie here, many Republicans moved from mass graves without their families' consent; exhumations in the crypts continue.
madrid-05.st: Franco ordered this basilica cut into the granite of the Guadarrama as a monument to his victory. Built from 1940 to 1959, partly by political prisoners, it received the remains of dead from both sides, many Republicans moved from mass graves without their families' consent. Franco was exhumed in 2019 and José Antonio Primo de Rivera in 2023; the Democratic Memory Law renamed the valley, and forensic exhumations continue. Today visitors see the esplanade, the rock-cut basilica and the great cross.

madrid-06.ev: Prisoners taken from Madrid prisons are shot here in the largest single massacre in the Republican zone.
madrid-06.rem: Officers, priests and conservatives taken from Madrid's prisons lie in these mass graves; responsibility for the orders is still debated.
madrid-06.st: In November 1936, as Nationalist troops reached Madrid, thousands of prisoners, among them officers, priests, Falangists and conservatives, were taken from the city's prisons in 'sacas' and shot here and at Soto de Aldovea. It was the largest single massacre in the Republican zone. The orders came from Madrid's public-order authorities; the responsibility of Santiago Carrillo and the role of Soviet advisers remain contested. Today a walled cemetery holds rows of mass graves, crosses and plaques naming identified victims.

madrid-07.ev: Madrid's first skyscraper serves as the Republic's observation post and press office under shellfire.

q.t: What was the stretch of Gran Vía outside the Telefónica nicknamed?
q.x: Nationalist guns on Garabitas hill struck the tower again and again, so the Gran Vía outside became known as 'Shell Alley'.

madrid-07.rem: Despite repeated shelling, the telephone exchange here never stopped working.
madrid-07.st: Madrid's first skyscraper, completed in 1929, was the Republic's eye over the front, its observers watching Nationalist movements in the Casa de Campo. It housed the telephone exchange and the Foreign Press Office, where Hemingway and Dos Passos filed censored reports. Nationalist guns on Garabitas hit it again and again, yet the exchange never stopped working, and the street outside became 'Shell Alley'. Today the restored tower dominates Gran Vía and hosts free exhibitions.

madrid-08.ev: Picasso paints Guernica for the Republic's pavilion at the 1937 Paris International Exhibition.

q.t: Why did Guernica stay in New York for decades?
o: Picasso wanted it in Spain only after democracy returned
Spain refused to pay for it
It was too fragile to travel
q.x: Picasso wanted the painting to go to Spain only when democracy returned; MoMA handed it over in September 1981.

madrid-08.rem: Guernica responds to the bombing of the Basque town by the Condor Legion and Italian aircraft on 26 April 1937.
madrid-08.st: Picasso painted Guernica for the Republic's pavilion at the 1937 Paris International Exhibition, in response to the bombing of the Basque town by the Condor Legion and Italian aircraft. After the war the Museum of Modern Art in New York kept it, because Picasso wanted it to go to Spain only when democracy returned. It came to Spain in 1981 and to the Reina Sofía in 1992. Today it hangs with its sketches, among rooms of Civil War posters and photographs.

madrid-09.ev: Varela's troops take Garabitas hill and hold it for the rest of the war.

q.t: What did the Nationalist batteries on Garabitas shell from December 1936?
o: Madrid's city centre and the Telefónica
q.x: From December 1936 the batteries on Garabitas shelled the city centre, the Gran Vía and the Telefónica building.

madrid-09.rem: The front across the Casa de Campo stayed almost static until March 1939, and bunkers of both sides survive in the woods.
madrid-09.st: Garabitas is one of the highest points of the Casa de Campo, the former royal hunting estate through which Nationalist columns attacked Madrid in November 1936. Varela's troops took the hill on 13 November and held it for the rest of the war despite Republican counter-attacks, including by the XI International Brigade. Their batteries here shelled the city centre and the Telefónica building. Today the summit offers a panoramic view over Madrid, with bunkers scattered through the park.

madrid-10.ev: Nationalist sappers build concrete machine-gun posts under fire facing the University City front.

q.t: How many of the Nationalist machine-gun posts here survive?
q.x: Of around twenty such posts, three survive, protected as heritage; one carries the inscription 'Zapadores nº 7'.

madrid-10.rem: These bunkers are among the few tangible traces of the siege line inside Madrid itself.
madrid-10.st: The northern end of the Parque del Oeste lay on the front line facing the Nationalist salient in the University City. Nationalist sappers built concrete machine-gun posts here under fire, and the stages of construction still show in the concrete; one carries the inscription 'Zapadores nº 7'. Of around twenty such posts, three survive, protected as heritage, among the few tangible traces of the siege line inside the city itself. Today the three sealed bunkers stand quietly among the park's trees and lawns.

madrid-11.ev: Republican militias and International Brigades defend the railway bridge against the Nationalist drive on Madrid.

q.t: Where did the Nationalists finally cross the Manzanares instead?
o: Further north, into the University City
At the Puente de los Franceses
q.x: The bridge held; the Nationalists crossed the river further north and entered the University City.

madrid-11.rem: The defence of this bridge inspired the Republican song 'Puente de los Franceses, mamita mía, nadie te pasa'.
madrid-11.st: This 19th-century railway bridge over the Manzanares was one of the crossings the Nationalists needed to break into Madrid from the Casa de Campo in November 1936. Republican militias and troops, soon joined by the newly arrived International Brigades, defended it, and the fighting is remembered as part of the Brigades' baptism of fire. It gave its name to a popular Republican song, and the Nationalists eventually crossed the river further north instead. Today the original brick-and-granite five-arch bridge still carries trains.

madrid-12.ev: Armed workers and loyal troops storm the Montaña barracks, where General Fanjul had risen.

q.t: What stands today on the site of the Montaña barracks?
q.x: The ruined barracks were demolished after the war, and the Egyptian Temple of Debod was re-erected on the site in 1972.

madrid-12.rem: The fall of the barracks secured Madrid for the Republic; many inside were killed after the surrender.
madrid-12.st: Here stood the Montaña barracks, where General Joaquín Fanjul rose for the coup in Madrid on 19 July 1936 and was then besieged. On 20 July armed workers, Assault Guards and loyal troops stormed it; many officers and soldiers inside were killed after the surrender, and Fanjul was later tried and shot. The fall of the barracks secured Madrid for the Republic. Today the Egyptian Temple of Debod stands in a park on the site, with no trace of the barracks.

madrid-13.ev: Republican engineers dig 'Posición Jaca', the command bunker of Miaja's Army of the Centre.

q.t: Whose command bunker was Posición Jaca?
o: General Miaja's Army of the Centre
q.x: It was the command bunker of General Miaja's Army of the Centre and his chief of staff Vicente Rojo, completed in August 1937.

madrid-13.rem: Some 15 m underground, it is one of the best-preserved Civil War command posts in Spain.
madrid-13.st: Beneath the 18th-century garden of the Dukes of Osuna, Republican engineers dug 'Posición Jaca', the command bunker of General Miaja's Army of the Centre and his chief of staff Vicente Rojo, completed in August 1937. Its central gallery had rooms for about 200 people, generators and gas-proof doors. It is one of Spain's best-preserved Civil War command posts and shows how the defence of Madrid was run. Today visitors walk its restored galleries beneath El Capricho.

madrid-14.ev: Republican troops and International Brigades stop Varela's Jarama crossing short of the Madrid–Valencia road.

q.t: Who built up this museum's collection?
o: Local enthusiasts, veterans and their families
The International Brigades association in London
q.x: The small private museum was built up by local enthusiasts, with objects recovered from the battlefield or donated by veterans and families.

madrid-14.rem: The battle cost many thousands of casualties on each side; this museum is the natural starting point for the battlefield.
madrid-14.st: In February 1937 Nationalist forces under Varela crossed the Jarama, and Republican troops, with the International Brigades, stopped them short of the Madrid–Valencia road at a cost of many thousands of casualties on each side. This small private museum, built up by local enthusiasts, gathers thousands of objects recovered from the battlefield or donated by veterans and their families, from rifles and pierced helmets to ration cards. It is the natural starting point for the battlefield. Today its rooms display battlefield finds, maps and photographs.

madrid-15.ev: Volunteers of many nations fight on the Jarama; memorials to them rise decades later.
madrid-15.rem: For decades the Brigades could not be commemorated in Spain; Chirino's clasped hands honour all who fought in this battle.
madrid-15.st: In February 1937 British, Irish, American, Balkan and Franco-Belgian volunteers fought on the Jarama. For decades after 1939 the International Brigades could not be commemorated in Spain. After the return of democracy, associations and veterans' families raised memorials along the Morata–San Martín de la Vega road, and a sculpture by Martín Chirino of two clasped hands, on the Casas Altas hill, honours all who fought in the battle. Today memorial stones line the road, and the sculpture stands among trenches.

madrid-16.ev: The Republic's first great offensive takes Brunete, but Nationalist counter-attacks retake it on 24 July.

q.t: Which division took Brunete by surprise on the first day?
q.x: Líster's 11th Division took Brunete on 6 July, but the attack stalled and Varela's counter-offensive retook the village.

madrid-16.rem: Brunete was flattened in the fighting; the parish church still shows bullet and shrapnel impacts.
madrid-16.st: On 6 July 1937 the Republic launched its first great offensive west of Madrid, aiming to cut off the Nationalist troops besieging the capital. Líster's 11th Division took Brunete by surprise, but the attack stalled at Villanueva de la Cañada and Quijorna and in the July heat. Varela's counter-offensive, backed by the Condor Legion, retook Brunete on 24 July, and the flattened village was rebuilt after the war. Today the parish church still bears bullet and shrapnel marks.

madrid-17.ev: Republican forces rout Mussolini's Corpo Truppe Volontarie advancing on Guadalajara.

q.t: Who fought the Italian Blackshirts at the Palacio de Ibarra?
q.x: The Garibaldi Battalion of the XII International Brigade fought Italian Blackshirts on 13–14 March: Italians against Italians.

madrid-17.rem: Rain grounded the Italian aircraft on muddy airfields while Republican planes flew from paved runways.
madrid-17.st: In March 1937 Mussolini's Corpo Truppe Volontarie under General Roatta drove towards Guadalajara to encircle Madrid, while rain grounded its aircraft. At the Palacio de Ibarra the Italian anti-fascist Garibaldi Battalion of the XII International Brigade fought Italian Blackshirts, Italians against Italians. On 18 March Republican divisions under Líster, Mera and others retook Brihuega. It became the Republic's most celebrated victory, magnified by its propaganda. Today Brihuega's walled old town stands above the Tajuña, with the palace ruins on private land nearby.

madrid-18.ev: Rebel troops push towards Madrid's reservoirs and are stopped just short of them.

q.t: Who helped Republican forces fortify the positions near the reservoirs?
o: Workers of the Canal de Isabel II
q.x: Republican forces, helped by workers of the Canal de Isabel II, stopped the rebels just short of the reservoirs supplying Madrid.

madrid-18.rem: This was a front over Madrid's water supply; 26 positions of both armies are now signposted.
madrid-18.st: In late July 1936 rebel troops under Colonel García Escámez crossed the Somosierra and seized Paredes de Buitrago, close to the reservoirs that supplied Madrid with water. Republican forces, helped by Canal de Isabel II workers who fortified the positions, stopped them just short. The front then stayed here for the rest of the war, the Nationalist 72nd Division facing Republican mixed brigades across the valley. Today signposted trenches, nests and command posts of both armies can be walked.

madrid-19.ev: Columns sent by General Mola seize the Guadarrama pass and hold it against Madrid militias.

q.t: What did the victors rename the Guadarrama pass?
q.x: The pass was renamed Alto de los Leones by the victors; it was one of the first battlefields of the war.

madrid-19.rem: Both sides fortified this mountain crest, and their bunkers and shelters survive in the pine woods.
madrid-19.st: The Guadarrama pass, renamed Alto de los Leones by the victors, was one of the first battlefields of the war. Columns sent by General Mola seized it on 22 July 1936 and held it against militia columns from Madrid in bloody fighting. The front then settled along the crest, and both sides fortified the mountain with concrete bunkers and observation posts. Today a bunker stands behind the roadside restaurant at the pass, with trenches in the pine woods towards La Jarosa.

madrid-20.ev: After Madrid's fall, the Almudena cemetery wall becomes the city's main place of execution.
madrid-20.rem: Among those shot at this wall were the 'Trece Rosas', thirteen young women executed on 5 August 1939.
madrid-20.st: After Madrid fell in March 1939, the eastern wall of the Almudena cemetery became the city's main place of execution. Large numbers of people were shot there between 1939 and 1944, among them the 'Trece Rosas', thirteen young women executed on 5 August 1939. The adjoining Cementerio Civil holds the graves of Republican leaders such as Francisco Largo Caballero, Dolores Ibárruri and Pablo Iglesias. Today visitors find graves, plaques to the Trece Rosas and a memorial to the victims at the wall.

madrid-21.ev: Moroccan Regulares seize the Pindoque bridge at night, opening the Nationalist way across the Jarama.

q.t: What happened when Republicans tried to blow the Pindoque bridge?
q.x: A Republican attempt to blow the bridge failed and it survived the explosion, opening the way to Pingarrón and Suicide Hill.

madrid-21.rem: These crossings began the Jarama battle; restored Republican trenches from 1938 lie nearby on the Cerro del Melero.
madrid-21.st: The Nationalist offensive of February 1937 needed to cross the Jarama. On the night of 11 February Moroccan Regulares crept up to the Pindoque railway bridge and silently killed the International Brigade sentries; a Republican attempt to blow the bridge failed. Further south, Barrón's cavalry seized the Arganda road bridge, opening the way to Pingarrón and Suicide Hill. Today both bridges cross the river in the Parque Regional del Sureste, with restored Republican trenches on the Cerro del Melero.

madrid-22.ev: Quijorna's small Nationalist garrison holds out three days against the Republican Brunete offensive.

q.t: How long did Quijorna's garrison resist?
q.x: The small garrison held out for three days before falling on 9 July 1937, costing the attackers time they could not afford.

madrid-22.rem: Quijorna shows how small strongpoints blunted the Brunete offensive.
madrid-22.st: Quijorna was one of the Nationalist strongpoints that blunted the Republic's Brunete offensive. Its small garrison held out for three days against Republican divisions before falling on 9 July 1937, costing the attackers time they could not afford. Both sides then fortified the surrounding hills, and the farmhouse of Casa de los Llanos served as a Republican planning centre. Today a concrete bunker stands on the hill above the village, and remains of the Republican camp of La Peña survive nearby.

madrid-23.ev: The Republican drive stalls at Villanueva de la Cañada and on the Mosquito Ridge.

q.t: Where did the Republican drive towards Boadilla stall?
o: At the Puente de los Franceses
q.x: The drive stalled on the Mosquito Ridge, where British and American battalions suffered heavily under a scorching sun.

madrid-23.rem: The failure to take the ridge ended hopes of cutting the Nationalist lines west of Madrid.
madrid-23.st: Villanueva de la Cañada, held by a small Nationalist garrison, resisted the Brunete offensive through its first day and fell only on the night of 7 July 1937, after the XV International Brigade and other units had been pinned down in open wheatfields. North-east of it the Republican drive stalled on Mosquito Ridge, where the British and American battalions suffered heavily under a scorching sun. Today the ridge and open battlefield can be seen from the Villanueva del Pardillo–Boadilla area.

madrid-24.ev: Nationalist sappers build Blockhaus 13, the only completed blockhouse of a planned line.

q.t: How many domed machine-gun nests does Blockhaus 13 have?
q.x: It has four domed machine-gun nests linked by a central corridor, with an inner courtyard and a cistern.

madrid-24.rem: Designed to withstand heavy artillery and bombs, it was declared a Bien de Interés Cultural in 2019.
madrid-24.st: After the Battle of Brunete the western front of Madrid settled along the Perales valley. In late 1938 the Nationalist 71st Division began a line of large concrete blockhouses here, and Blockhaus 13, built by the 7th Sapper Battalion, was the only one completed. Designed to withstand heavy artillery and bombs, it has four domed machine-gun nests linked by a central corridor. Today it stands almost intact, protected since 2019 as a Bien de Interés Cultural.

madrid-25.ev: The last Republican militiamen and civilians shelter in the cathedral under bombardment before surrendering.

q.t: What was added to the cathedral during its 1940s restoration?
o: A new lantern tower over the crossing
q.x: The damaged cathedral was restored in the 1940s, when a new lantern tower was added over the crossing.

madrid-25.rem: The cathedral's roofs, crossing and organ were destroyed while besieged defenders sheltered inside.
madrid-25.st: In the autumn of 1936 Nationalist columns advancing from Aragon and Soria besieged Sigüenza. The last Republican militiamen, with civilians, took refuge in the cathedral and held out for several days under artillery and air bombardment before surrendering in mid-October. The cathedral was badly damaged: roofs and the crossing collapsed, sculpture was shattered and the 18th-century organ destroyed. It was restored in the 1940s. Today the fortress-like Romanesque–Gothic cathedral shows its post-war repairs and the new lantern tower over the crossing.

madrid-26.ev: Militiamen stage a mock execution of the Sacred Heart statue, then dynamite the monument.
madrid-26.rem: Anticlerical violence destroyed the first monument; the regime's larger rebuilding became a symbol of the 'crusade' narrative.
madrid-26.st: The hill at Getafe carried a monument to the Sacred Heart of Jesus consecrated in 1919. In the anticlerical violence of summer 1936, militiamen staged a mock 'execution' of the statue by firing squad for the press, and the monument was dynamited on 7 August. The Nationalists took the hill in November, and it stayed near the front until the war's end. Franco's regime later rebuilt a larger monument. Today it stands beside ruins of the original, with bullet marks on the walls.

madrid-27.ev: A triumphal arch is built to commemorate the Francoist victory in the University City battle.
madrid-27.rem: The arch is now debated under the memory laws; the avenue beneath was renamed Avenida de la Concordia in 2024.
madrid-27.st: This triumphal arch at the entrance to the University City was built in 1950–56 to commemorate the Francoist victory in the battle there, where the front had run from November 1936 to March 1939. Its Latin inscriptions praise Franco's army and the rebuilt university. Under the Democratic Memory laws it has become the subject of debate over re-signification, and the avenue beneath it was renamed in 2024. Today it can be seen from the Moncloa interchange but cannot be entered.

madrid-30.ev: Political prisoners build the Madrid–Burgos railway as forced labour, living in a camp here.
madrid-30.rem: This is one of the few camps in Spain whose remains of prisoner labour can still be seen.
madrid-30.st: After the war the regime used political prisoners as forced labour on public works under the scheme of 'redemption of sentences through work'. At Bustarviejo, between 1944 and 1952, prisoners built the Madrid–Burgos railway, living in a camp since studied by archaeologists. It is one of the few such camps in Spain whose remains can be seen, and complements Cuelgamuros as evidence of prison labour. Today foundations of three compounds, guard posts and a punishment cell remain near the railway.

madrid-28.ev: Nationalist troops take the village and later fortify the heights along the western front.

q.t: On which river did the front halt near Fresnedillas?
q.x: After the Nationalists took the village on 5 November 1936, the front halted on the Perales river.

madrid-28.rem: Machine-gun nests, trenches and vaulted shelters here formed part of Madrid's western front.
madrid-28.st: Nationalist troops took Fresnedillas de la Oliva on 5 November 1936 during the advance on Madrid. The front then halted on the Perales river and saw heavy fighting in December. In 1937 the Nationalists fortified the heights around the village with machine-gun nests, trenches and catenary-vaulted shelters, forming part of the western front of Madrid. Several of these positions, including those of Cota 960, lie along local paths. Today concrete machine-gun posts, connecting trenches and vaulted storage shelters can be visited around the village.

madrid-29.ev: Nationalist troops dig a static rear line into the gypsum hills south of Madrid.

q.t: What did archaeologists record at Los Yesares?
o: Four posts, trenches, rifle pits and a shelter
q.x: Archaeologists recorded four concrete-and-masonry posts, trenches, rifle pits and a shelter on a limestone hill.

madrid-29.rem: The site shows the static rear lines that followed the Jarama battle.
madrid-29.st: South of Madrid, between Pinto and Valdemoro, the Nationalist line running from the Cerro de los Ángeles to the Jarama was dug into the gypsum hills. At Los Yesares, archaeologists of the Comunidad de Madrid have recorded concrete-and-masonry posts, trenches, rifle pits and a shelter on a limestone hill. The site shows the static rear lines that followed the Jarama battle. Today four small fortins, trenches and a shelter survive on a low hill.

aragon-01.ev: Republican troops fight house by house into Belchite, which falls on 6 September.

q.t: What did Franco do with Belchite's ruins after the war?
o: Left them as a monument and built a new town alongside
q.x: Franco left the ruins as a monument and built a new Belchite next to them.

aragon-01.rem: Thousands of soldiers and civilians were inside the town; the Trujal now honours all who died in the battle.
aragon-01.st: In the Republican Zaragoza offensive of 1937 the Army of the East under General Sebastián Pozas, with the XI and XV International Brigades, turned on Belchite, where thousands of soldiers and civilians were inside. Republican troops fought house by house from 1 September, and the town fell on 6 September, with heavy losses on both sides. Franco later left the ruins as a monument beside a new town. Today shell-scarred churches and roofless streets remain, with a memorial to all who died.

aragon-02.ev: Republican forces encircle and take Teruel, then lose it to Franco's counter-offensive in blizzards.

q.t: When did Colonel Rey d'Harcourt surrender Teruel's garrison?
q.x: Rey d'Harcourt surrendered on 8 January 1938; Franco's counter-offensive retook the ruined city on 22 February.

aragon-02.rem: Fought in temperatures down to about −18°C, Teruel was the war's harshest battle.
aragon-02.st: On 15 December 1937 the Republican Army of the Levante under Hernández Saravia, with Líster's and El Campesino's divisions, encircled Teruel. Colonel Domingo Rey d'Harcourt's garrison, with many civilians, held out in a few strongpoints until he surrendered on 8 January 1938. The battle was fought in blizzards and bitter cold, and Franco's counter-offensive under Aranda and Varela retook the ruined city on 22 February, after immense losses on both sides. Today wartime air-raid shelters lie beneath the old town.

aragon-03.ev: George Orwell serves with the POUM militia on the static Sierra de Alcubierre front.

q.t: In which book did Orwell describe this front?
q.x: Orwell described the cold, the lice and the stalemate in Homage to Catalonia (1938).

aragon-03.rem: The Aragon front here hardly moved for more than a year until the Nationalist offensive of March 1938.
aragon-03.st: From late 1936 the Aragon front ran across the bare Sierra de Alcubierre, where anarchist and POUM militias faced Nationalist positions such as San Simón and the line hardly moved for more than a year. George Orwell served here with the POUM militia until 16 February 1937 and described the cold, the lice and the stalemate in Homage to Catalonia. The front broke in March 1938. Today rebuilt Republican trenches, shelters and a bivouac line on Monte Irazo can be walked.

aragon-04.ev: People held for their political views are shot here and thrown into the well.
aragon-04.rem: Families and associations campaigned for decades to have the victims of this well remembered and identified.
aragon-04.st: Beside an old inn near Concud lies a well about 50 m deep. From July 1936 until the Republican encirclement of Teruel in December 1937, people held for their political views in Nationalist-held Teruel were shot here and their bodies placed in the well; when it was full, pits were dug nearby. Most sources attribute the killings to the Nationalist rearguard, and the number of victims is not established. Today the covered well is surrounded by family plaques and several memorials.

aragon-05.ev: Republican troops storm this fortified hill, which becomes a key position in the Teruel struggle.

q.t: What does El Muletón command?
o: The road north and the Alfambra valley
q.x: The steep hill north-west of Teruel commands the road north and the Alfambra valley.

aragon-05.rem: Shell and bomb craters from January 1938 are still visible near the Gilochas ravine.
aragon-05.st: El Muletón is a steep hill north-west of Teruel commanding the road north and the Alfambra valley. The Nationalists fortified it as part of the city's outer defences, with trenches, shelters and a concrete cistern. Republican troops stormed it early in the December 1937 offensive, and it became a key position in the struggle for Teruel, pounded by Nationalist artillery and aircraft in January 1938. Today a command post, the cistern, trenches and bomb craters survive.

aragon-06.ev: Franco's army breaks the Republican front in the Alfambra valley north of Teruel.

q.t: What was notable about the Nationalist attack in the Alfambra valley?
q.x: The attack included a Nationalist cavalry charge often called one of the last great cavalry charges in Western Europe.

aragon-06.rem: The breakthrough cut off the Republican salient and prepared the retaking of Teruel two weeks later.
aragon-06.st: In early February 1938 Franco's army broke the Republican front north of Teruel in the Alfambra valley, overrunning several villages and taking thousands of prisoners. The attack included a charge by Nationalist cavalry, often called one of the last great cavalry charges in Western Europe. The breakthrough cut off the Republican salient north of the city and prepared the retaking of Teruel two weeks later. Today the centre explains the battle with maps, photographs and objects, linked to nearby trenches.

aragon-07.ev: Robres lies just behind the Republican Sierra de Alcubierre front held by militia columns.

q.t: Which nearby trench route pairs naturally with the Robres centre?
q.x: The centre covers the militia war and the static front, and pairs naturally with the Ruta Orwell trenches in the nearby hills.

aragon-07.rem: The centre also covers the collectives and social revolution in the Republican rear.
aragon-07.st: Robres lay just behind the Republican side of the Sierra de Alcubierre front, held from 1936 to 1938 by anarchist CNT-FAI and POUM militia columns and later by the Popular Army. The village's centre covers the militia war and the static front, the collectives and social revolution in the Republican rear, and the Nationalist breakthrough of March 1938. Today its rooms display panels, photographs, weapons and everyday objects from the front, alongside a documentation centre.

aragon-08.ev: The Republican 35th Division storms Quinto and its fortified hills.

q.t: Which division stormed Quinto in August 1937?
q.x: The Republican 35th Division, including the XV International Brigade, took Quinto; the last defenders surrendered on 26 August.

aragon-08.rem: Quinto then served as a Republican headquarters until March 1938.
aragon-08.st: Quinto was a fortified Nationalist outpost on the Ebro, its main strongpoint on the Purburel and Cabezo de la Nariz hills behind wire, trenches and concrete works. On 24–26 August 1937 the Republican 35th Division, including the XV International Brigade with its British, American and Dimitrov battalions, stormed the town and hills. The last defenders surrendered on 26 August, and Quinto became a Republican headquarters. Today about 250 m of excavated trenches and dugouts overlook the Ebro plain.

aragon-09.ev: Thousands are shot at the walls of Torrero cemetery during the war and post-war years.
aragon-09.rem: A monument stands over the common grave found in 1979; the cemetery also holds graves of the Nationalist fallen.
aragon-09.st: Zaragoza fell to the military rising on 19 July 1936 without a fight and became the Nationalists' main base on the Aragon front. Repression there was carried out mainly at the walls of Torrero cemetery, where thousands were shot in the war and post-war years; the full number is still being researched. In 1980 the city's first democratic mayor dedicated a monument over a common grave found the year before. Today that memorial stands near a Nationalist memorial chapel.

aragon-10.ev: A Republican aircraft bombs the Basilica del Pilar, and none of the bombs explode.

q.t: How did Nationalist propaganda present the unexploded bombs?
q.x: Nationalist propaganda presented it as a miracle; two of the bombs are still displayed inside the basilica.

aragon-10.rem: The bombs became a strong symbol of the religious meaning Franco's side gave its war.
aragon-10.st: Early in the war a Republican aircraft attacked Nationalist-held Zaragoza and dropped bombs on the Basilica of Our Lady of the Pillar, Spain's great Marian shrine. The bombs fell on the church and the square beside it, and none exploded; accounts differ on how many there were. Nationalist propaganda presented this as a miracle, and it became a strong symbol of the religious meaning Franco's side gave its war. Today two defused bombs hang on a pillar inside the basilica.

aragon-11.ev: Italian bombers flying for the Nationalists strike Alcañiz's town centre and market area.
aragon-11.rem: The raid struck a town more than 70 km from the front; the shelter now remembers its victims.
aragon-11.st: Alcañiz council built this shelter in 1937 for about 230 residents of the Almudines quarter. On 3 March 1938 bombers of the Italian Aviazione Legionaria, flying for the Nationalists, attacked the town centre and market area, far from the front. It was one of the deadliest raids on a town in Aragon, and the number of dead and missing remains uncertain. Days later the Nationalist Aragon offensive swept through the region. Today the underground gallery holds an exhibition on the raid and its victims.

aragon-12.ev: Anarchist militias kill clergy in Barbastro, including 51 Claretian missionaries and the bishop.
aragon-12.rem: Most of the 51 Claretians were young seminarians; their letters and belongings are kept here.
aragon-12.st: Barbastro stayed in Republican hands after the rising. In the first weeks of the war anarchist militias carried out one of the worst killings of clergy in the Republican zone here, among the dead 51 Claretian missionaries, mostly young seminarians, other religious and diocesan priests, and Bishop Florentino Asensio. The diocese lost a larger share of its clergy than any other in Spain. Today a museum in the Claretian house keeps the seminarians' letters and belongings, and a crypt holds their remains.

aragon-13.ev: Catalan Carlist volunteers hold encircled Codo until survivors break out.

q.t: Who defended Codo in August 1937?
o: The Tercio de Nuestra Señora de Montserrat
q.x: Codo was held by the Tercio de Nuestra Señora de Montserrat, Catalan Carlist volunteers, with other troops; survivors broke out on 25 August.

aragon-13.rem: The battalion suffered such losses that it ceased to exist as a fighting unit.
aragon-13.st: At the start of the Zaragoza offensive the Republican 25th Division attacked the small village of Codo, between Belchite and Quinto. It was held by the Tercio de Nuestra Señora de Montserrat, a battalion of Catalan Carlist volunteers, with other troops. Encircled on 24 August 1937, the defenders fought on until the survivors broke out the next day. The battalion suffered very heavy losses, though published figures differ. Today the rebuilt village has a commemorative cross to the fallen requetés.

aragon-14.ev: Republican units take the fortified hilltop church after bitter fighting.

q.t: What did restoration uncover inside El Piquete church?
q.x: Restoration uncovered 18th-century mummified burials, 'las momias de Quinto', now displayed in the church.

aragon-14.rem: Civilians sheltered inside the church alongside its defenders during the fighting.
aragon-14.st: The old parish church called 'El Piquete' stands on the Cerro de la Corona above Quinto. In August 1937 about 300 Nationalist defenders turned it into a fortress, and civilians also sheltered inside. The XV International Brigade and other Republican units took it after bitter house-to-house fighting and artillery fire that badly damaged the tower. Most of the town was destroyed and rebuilt after the war. Today the battle-scarred church still stands, with 18th-century mummified burials displayed inside.

aragon-15.ev: Republican forces build a machine-gun bunker to control the Huesca–Barbastro road.
aragon-15.rem: The siege lines around Nationalist-held Huesca lasted until March 1938.
aragon-15.st: After July 1936 Nationalist-held Huesca was almost surrounded by Republican columns, and the siege lines lasted until March 1938. In late 1936 Republican forces under Colonel Villalba built this machine-gun bunker to control the Huesca–Barbastro road. The front saw costly Republican attacks, above all the June 1937 offensive in which General Lukács of the XII International Brigade was killed; George Orwell was wounded here in May 1937. Today the well-preserved bunker stands beside the old road.

aragon-16.ev: The medieval castle-abbey forms part of the Republican ring around Nationalist-held Huesca.

q.t: What ended the Republican siege lines around Huesca?
q.x: The front moved away only when the Nationalist offensive of March 1938 broke the siege lines.

aragon-16.rem: Its commanding views over Huesca made the castle an important Republican observation post.
aragon-16.st: The 11th-century castle-abbey of Montearagón stands on a hill east of Huesca. According to the regional heritage record, from 1936 to 1938 it formed part of the Republican ring around Nationalist-held Huesca, together with the Estrecho Quinto bunker below. Its views over the city made it an important observation and defensive position until the Nationalist offensive of March 1938 broke the siege lines. Today its massive medieval walls look out over Huesca and the old siege ground.

aragon-17.ev: Republicans fortify the heights east of Teruel, with Alto de la Torana as the strongest point.

q.t: What did Alto de la Torana control?
q.x: Alto de la Torana was the strongest point of the Republican line and controlled the old road into Teruel.

aragon-17.rem: The site is one of 17 Civil War sites restored on the 'Atrinchérate' route around Teruel.
aragon-17.st: East of Teruel the Republicans built a fortified line on the heights around Corbalán after militia columns reached the area in summer 1936. Alto de la Torana was its strongest point, controlling the old road into Teruel. The nearby Cabigordo trenches saw heavy fighting in the last phase of the Battle of Teruel. Today the restored site, on the 'Atrinchérate' route, has a well-kept machine-gun post, trenches, a shelter and a deep command bunker cut into the rock.

aragon-18.ev: The cut-off Republican 43rd Division holds the Bielsa Pocket while civilians cross into France.

q.t: What did most of the 43rd Division's men do after crossing into France?
o: Returned to Republican Catalonia to keep fighting
q.x: After holding the pocket for about two months, the soldiers crossed in mid-June 1938; most went back to Republican Catalonia.

aragon-18.rem: Thousands of civilians fled over the Pyrenean passes, and Bielsa itself was largely destroyed.
aragon-18.st: When the Nationalist Aragon offensive broke the front in spring 1938, the Republican 43rd Division under Antonio Beltrán was cut off in the high Pyrenean valley of Bielsa. For about two months it held the pocket against far larger forces while thousands of civilians crossed the passes into France. In mid-June the soldiers followed, and most returned to Republican Catalonia to keep fighting. Bielsa was largely destroyed. Today the village museum tells the story of the pocket and the exodus.

aragon-19.ev: International Brigades defend Caspe against Yagüe's divisions until the town falls on 17 March.

q.t: What body had its seat in Caspe from 1936?
o: The Nationalist Army of the North
The Regional Defence Council of Aragon
q.x: Caspe was the seat of the anarchist-led Regional Defence Council of Aragon, dissolved by the Republican government in August 1937.

aragon-19.rem: After its fall Caspe became a Nationalist corps headquarters for the Ebro front.
aragon-19.st: From 1936 Caspe was the seat of the anarchist-led Regional Defence Council of Aragon, dissolved by force by the Republican government in August 1937. During the Aragon offensive three divisions of Yagüe's Moroccan Army Corps reached Caspe on 15 March 1938. International Brigades defended the town, the XV Brigade most stubbornly, until it fell on 17 March and became a Nationalist headquarters for the Ebro front. Today the historic centre and surrounding hills hold scattered, mostly unmarked traces.

aragon-20.ev: A Republican tank attack with International Brigade infantry breaks down before Fuentes de Ebro.

q.t: Which battalion saw its first major action at Fuentes de Ebro?
q.x: The Canadian Mackenzie-Papineau Battalion was in its first major action; the poorly coordinated attack broke down.

aragon-20.rem: Poor coordination between tanks, infantry and artillery cost the attack; the town stayed in Nationalist hands.
aragon-20.st: As the last act of the Zaragoza offensive, on 13 October 1937 the Republicans attacked the fortified town of Fuentes de Ebro. Soviet-built BT-5 tanks charged with XV International Brigade infantry riding on them or following behind, including the Canadian Mackenzie-Papineau Battalion in its first major action. Poorly coordinated, the attack broke down with heavy losses in tanks and men, and the town stayed in Nationalist hands. Today the open, flat fields of the attack show few visible remains.

aragon-21.ev: The Popular Army builds a fortified line south of Teruel, including this observation post.

q.t: What could observers see from inside the Aldehuela bunker?
q.x: The concrete observation post faced Nationalist positions, and from inside observers could see Teruel itself.

aragon-21.rem: It is one of the few pieces of the Republican line south of Teruel to survive intact.
aragon-21.st: Before the Battle of Teruel the Popular Army built a fortified line south of the city, facing Nationalist positions such as the Muela de Villaspesa. This concrete observation post, on the hill opposite Aldehuela cemetery, is one of the few pieces of that line to survive intact. From inside it, Republican observers could see Teruel itself across the valley. Today the domed bunker, with stepped courses left by its formwork, is entered through a tunnel in the slope.

aragon-22.ev: Republicans fortify the Mansueto promontory with a small concrete-and-brick fort.

q.t: What held up the concrete roof of the Mansueto fort?
q.x: Instead of sandbagged trenches, the Republicans built a small fort roofed with a concrete slab on railway rails.

aragon-22.rem: The fort formed part of the Republican ring around Teruel.
aragon-22.st: Mansueto is a promontory above Valdecebro guarding the south-eastern approach to Teruel. The Republicans fortified it not with the usual sandbagged trenches but with a small fort of thick concrete and brick walls, roofed with a concrete slab laid on railway rails. It formed part of the Republican ring around Teruel in 1937 and 1938, and its solid construction set it apart from most positions on this front. Today broken wall sections with firing loopholes and fragments of the concrete roof remain on the promontory.

aragon-23.ev: A defence line on the ridge above the prison watches the Turia riverbed below Teruel.

q.t: Which area was the Las Viñas sector around?
q.x: The Las Viñas sector around Teruel cemetery was contested from the very start of the war.

aragon-23.rem: This concrete fort served as observatory, rifle post and bunker on the edge of Teruel.
aragon-23.st: The Las Viñas sector around Teruel cemetery was contested from the very start of the war. A defence line on the ridge above the prison watched the Turia riverbed and the old Zaragoza road below the city. This concrete observation fort and bunker, on the edge of Teruel itself, is one of the surviving pieces of that line. Today the thick-walled fort, which served as an observatory, a rifle post and a bunker, can still be seen.

aragon-24.ev: Defenders of this fortified hill dig a tunnel to move unseen from the trench line.

q.t: Why did the defenders dig a tunnel to the back of the hill?
o: To move without being seen or hit
q.x: The tunnel let the defenders move without being seen or hit from the Republican positions at Las Cañadas.

aragon-24.rem: Which side held the Muela is not confirmed by the sources.
aragon-24.st: The Muela de Villaspesa was an intermediate fortified point south of Teruel, overlooking the Republican positions at Aldehuela and the Turia valley. Its defenders dug a tunnel from the trench line to the back of the hill so they could move without being seen or hit from the Republican positions at Las Cañadas. Which side held the hill is not confirmed by the available source, although the layout suggests the Nationalists. Today trenches and observation posts face Aldehuela, and the tunnel's rear entrance is sealed.

catalonia-01.ev: Corbera is pounded by artillery and aircraft throughout the 115 days of the Ebro battle.

q.t: What happened to Corbera's inhabitants after the war?
o: They never returned, and a new village was built below
q.x: The inhabitants never returned; a new village was built below, and the ruins became a memorial to all victims of the battle.

catalonia-01.rem: The ruins were declared a Bé Cultural d'Interès in 1993 as a memorial to all victims of the battle.
catalonia-01.st: The old hilltop village of Corbera d'Ebre lay on the road junction between Gandesa and the Ebro crossings. After the Republican Army of the Ebro crossed the river in July 1938, Corbera was pounded by Nationalist artillery and the German and Italian air forces, and fighting swept back through it in the autumn counter-offensives. The inhabitants never returned, and a new village was built below. Today roofless streets climb to the shell-scarred church of Sant Pere, with a plaque to the British Battalion.

catalonia-02.ev: Republican troops hold the bare Pàndols ridge against repeated Nationalist assaults.

q.t: Why was fighting on the Pàndols ridge so hard?
o: Men fought on bare rock where trenches could barely be dug
q.x: The ridge is bare limestone: trenches could barely be dug and the dead often could not be buried.

catalonia-02.rem: The ridge was the southern bastion of the Ebro bridgehead and held until the autumn collapse.
catalonia-02.st: The bare limestone ridge of Pàndols was the southern bastion of the Ebro bridgehead. Republican troops, including Líster's 5th Army Corps and the 35th Division with the XV International Brigade, held it through August 1938 against repeated Nationalist assaults backed by massive artillery and air bombardment. Men fought on bare rock where trenches could barely be dug and the dead often could not be buried. Today a memorial, stone parapets and scraped rifle pits stand near the summit.

catalonia-03.ev: Republican units reach Gandesa's outskirts but never take the town, the pivot of the battle.

q.t: What was the museum building used for in 1938?
q.x: The museum is housed in a former school that served as a blood hospital in 1938.

catalonia-03.rem: Gandesa was the prize the Republican offensive never took.
catalonia-03.st: Gandesa was the prize the Republican offensive never took. After crossing the Ebro on 25 July 1938, Republican units reached the outskirts within days but were stopped by Nationalist reinforcements, and the town became the pivot of the whole battle. The museum occupies a former school that served as a blood hospital in 1938 and gives the best overview before visiting the field. Today its exhibition shows weapons, uniforms, models, a reconstructed trench and a field-hospital ward.

catalonia-04.ev: Poble-sec residents dig their own shelter against the air raids on Barcelona.

q.t: What was Refugi 307 used for after the war?
q.x: After the war the shelter was used to grow mushrooms and later as makeshift housing.

catalonia-04.rem: Shelters like this, dug by residents themselves, saved many lives during the 1938 raids.
catalonia-04.st: Barcelona was bombed around 200 times during the war, mostly by Italian aircraft flying from Mallorca, with German participation. From 1937 the residents of Poble-sec, a working-class district near the port, dug this shelter themselves, with water, a first-aid room, toilets and a children's area. Shelters like this saved many lives during the raids of 1938, including three days in March when a great many people were killed. Today visitors walk the original galleries dug into the Montjuïc slope.

catalonia-05.ev: An old quarry becomes the common grave for people executed after Barcelona falls.
catalonia-05.rem: The names of the executed are listed on the stone columns; President Lluís Companys lies in the mausoleum here.
catalonia-05.st: This old quarry in Montjuïc cemetery became a common grave for people executed by the Franco regime after Barcelona fell in January 1939, most of them shot at the Camp de la Bóta; bombing victims and the city's poorest were also buried here. Lluís Companys, President of the Generalitat, shot at Montjuïc castle in 1940, lies in the mausoleum. The site became a memorial in 1985. Today a quiet sunken garden holds stone columns listing the victims' names.

catalonia-06.ev: The Republican anti-aircraft battery fires on bombers raiding Barcelona from this hill.

q.t: What occupied the gun emplacements after the war until 1990?
q.x: After the war the emplacements were taken over by shanty housing, which remained until 1990.

catalonia-06.rem: The site explains two chapters: wartime air defence and post-war shanty life.
catalonia-06.st: The Republican anti-aircraft defence built its main battery on this hill because it commanded the city. Four Vickers guns, directed by acoustic locators and searchlights, fired on the Italian and German bombers raiding Barcelona in 1937 and 1938. They were disabled as the Republicans withdrew in January 1939. After the war shanty housing occupied the emplacements until 1990, and in 2011 the city history museum restored the site. Today gun platforms and shanty floor tiles sit above a 360° view of Barcelona.

catalonia-07.ev: Italian aircraft bomb the square; a second bomb strikes as rescuers dig out survivors.
catalonia-07.rem: Forty-two people died here, most of them children; the shrapnel scars on the church remain.
catalonia-07.st: On 30 January 1938 Italian aircraft from Mallorca bombed the old city of Barcelona. One bomb fell on this small square, where the church crypt served as a shelter for the neighbouring school and for children evacuated from Madrid. As rescuers dug survivors from the rubble, a second bomb struck. Forty-two people were killed, most of them children. For decades the damage was said to come from executions. Today the façade is still pitted with shrapnel scars, and a plaque remembers the victims.

catalonia-08.ev: Civilians and defeated soldiers flee over the French border in the Retirada.

q.t: Where did France hold many of the refugees?
o: In improvised camps on beaches such as Argelès
q.x: France held many refugees in improvised camps on beaches such as Argelès and Saint-Cyprien.

catalonia-08.rem: The exodus crossed in winter, under air attack, through the border towns and mountain passes.
catalonia-08.st: As Nationalist forces overran Catalonia after the fall of Barcelona in January 1939, a huge mass of civilians and defeated soldiers fled north to France in the Retirada. They crossed the border and the mountain passes in winter and under air attack, and France held many of them in improvised beach camps such as Argelès and Saint-Cyprien. The MUME, opened here in 2008, tells the story of this exodus and of exile. Today its exhibition presents photographs, objects and testimonies.

catalonia-09.ev: Negrín holds the last session of the Republican Cortes on Spanish soil in the castle stables.
catalonia-09.rem: The last Cortes met here; from 1940 to 1942 the castle held Republicans returned from France in a concentration camp.
catalonia-09.st: As Catalonia collapsed, the Republican government withdrew to Figueres. On 1 February 1939 Prime Minister Juan Negrín held the last session of the Republican Cortes on Spanish soil in the stables of this fortress, proposing peace conditions that Franco ignored. Days later the government crossed into France, and Nationalist troops reached the border on 10 February. From 1940 to 1942 the regime used the castle as a concentration camp. Today visitors can see the stables where the Cortes met, the bastions and cisterns.

catalonia-10.ev: The final Nationalist offensive breaks through at La Fatarella, ending the Ebro bridgehead.

q.t: Where did the last Republican units recross the Ebro on 16 November?
q.x: After the breakthrough at La Fatarella, the last Republican units recrossed the river at Flix on 16 November, ending the battle.

catalonia-10.rem: The Serra de la Fatarella was the last stronghold of the Republican Ebro bridgehead.
catalonia-10.st: The Serra de la Fatarella was the northern shoulder of the Republican Ebro bridgehead and its last stronghold. Les Devees was a rear position guarding the approach to La Fatarella, where soldiers built two shelters, one in an old lime kiln, joined to a zig-zag trench. In mid-November 1938 the final Nationalist offensive broke through here, and the last Republican units recrossed the river on 16 November, ending the battle. Today the restored shelters and trench are explained by panels.

catalonia-11.ev: The Camposines crossroads is fought over in the final weeks of the Ebro battle.
catalonia-11.rem: The ossuary receives remains of soldiers of both armies still being found across the battlefield, most of them unknown.
catalonia-11.st: The Camposines crossroads, on the road from the Ebro crossings towards Gandesa, was a key junction behind the Republican front and was fought over in the battle's final weeks. In 2009 the Generalitat built a memorial here over the line of an old trench. It serves as an ossuary for the remains of soldiers of both armies still being found across the battlefield, most of them unidentified. Today the memorial stands beside the hermitage of Sant Bartomeu, looking towards the Ebro valley.

catalonia-12.ev: Republican attacks fail to take Vilalba dels Arcs on the northern edge of the advance.

q.t: What is special about the Els Barrancs trenches?
o: They are the best-preserved trench network in the Ebro heritage network
They were built by the International Brigades
q.x: Els Barrancs keeps about 700 m of trench line, the best-preserved network in the Ebro heritage network.

catalonia-12.rem: The 'Soldats a les trinxeres' centre explains everyday life of soldiers at the front.
catalonia-12.st: Vilalba dels Arcs lay on the northern edge of the Republican advance of 25 July 1938, and Republican attacks failed to take the village and its hills. The Mirador del Bassot looks over the ground where those assaults were made. Just outside the village, Els Barrancs keeps about 700 m of trench line with firing pits, shelters and huts, though sources are unclear on which army built it. Today the restored trenches can be walked, with a viewpoint in the village.

catalonia-14.ev: The Nationalist command watches the Battle of the Ebro from this hilltop post.

q.t: What lies beneath the Coll del Moro observation post?
q.x: The post was built on top of an Iberian settlement and necropolis; Franco himself came here to watch the battle.

catalonia-14.rem: The Nationalists relied on artillery and air superiority to wear down the bridgehead.
catalonia-14.st: From this hill west of Gandesa, built on top of an Iberian settlement and necropolis, the Nationalist command watched the Battle of the Ebro in 1938. Franco himself came here, as did senior commanders and foreign military observers. The Nationalist approach relied on artillery and air superiority to wear down the Republican bridgehead through a series of costly counter-offensives rather than manoeuvre. Today the observation post stands beside the excavated Iberian tower and settlement, with wide views from Gandesa to the Pàndols and Cavalls ridges.

catalonia-15.ev: Flix residents dig a shelter against repeated bombing; the Ebro battle begins and ends here.

q.t: Why was Flix bombed repeatedly?
o: It held a large chemical factory and a river crossing
q.x: Flix had a large chemical factory and a river crossing, so it was bombed repeatedly.

catalonia-15.rem: The last Republican troops withdrew across the river here on the night of 15–16 November 1938.
catalonia-15.st: Flix had a large chemical factory and a river crossing, and it was bombed repeatedly; its inhabitants dug this shelter under the old town. On 25 July 1938 Republican units of the XV Army Corps crossed the Ebro in this sector at the start of the offensive. On the night of 15–16 November the last Republican troops withdrew across the river here, ending the Battle of the Ebro. Today the restored galleries hold an exhibition on the bombing of Flix and on civil defence.

catalonia-16.ev: The Army of the Ebro crosses the river below the castle by boat and footbridge.

q.t: What was one Republican aim of the Ebro crossing?
q.x: The Republic aimed to relieve pressure on Valencia and restore the link with the central zone.

catalonia-16.rem: The crossing took the Nationalists by surprise in the early hours of 25 July 1938.
catalonia-16.st: The Templar castle of Miravet stands above one of the stretches where the Army of the Ebro crossed the river by boat and footbridge in the early hours of 25 July 1938, taking the Nationalists by surprise. The Republican aim was to relieve pressure on Valencia and restore the link with the central zone. The castle shows well how the river shaped the fighting. Today it houses a permanent exhibition on the battle, with views over the river and the village.

catalonia-18.ev: The fortress serves as prison and execution ground for whichever side holds Barcelona.
catalonia-18.rem: Both sides executed prisoners here; President Lluís Companys was shot in the moat on 15 October 1940.
catalonia-18.st: The fortress above the port served as a prison and execution ground for whichever side held Barcelona. In August 1936 the Republican authorities executed the rebel generals Manuel Goded and Álvaro Fernández Burriel here after the failed rising. After the city fell in 1939 the Franco regime used the castle as a prison, and on 15 October 1940 Lluís Companys, President of the Generalitat, was shot in its moat after a summary court-martial. Today a memorial marks the spot in the moat.

catalonia-20.ev: Police try to take the Telefónica from the CNT, sparking the May Days fighting in Barcelona.

q.t: Who ran the Telefónica exchange before 3 May 1937?
q.x: A CNT workers' committee had run the exchange since July 1936; the attempt to take it sparked the May Days.

catalonia-20.rem: The May Days pitted forces within the Republican camp against each other and led to the suppression of the POUM.
catalonia-20.st: On 3 May 1937 Catalan police under Eusebio Rodríguez Salas tried to take the Telefónica exchange from the CNT workers' committee that had run it since July 1936. The anarchists opened fire, and barricades went up across Barcelona as the CNT and POUM faced the Generalitat, the PSUC and government forces. After a ceasefire the government took control of public order; the POUM was later suppressed and Andreu Nin kidnapped and murdered. Today the Telefónica building still faces the square, without its dome.

catalonia-23.ev: A Republican-built airfield is captured and used by Nationalist squadrons and the Condor Legion.

q.t: Who built the La Sénia airfield?
o: The Republican Army, with Soviet machinery
q.x: The Republican Army built the airfield in 1936–37 with Soviet machinery; it was captured after April 1938.

catalonia-23.rem: Built by one side and used by the other, the airfield reflects how the Republic was cut in two in 1938.
catalonia-23.st: The Republican Army built this airfield in 1936–37 with Soviet machinery. After the Nationalist drive to the sea in April 1938 cut the Republic in two, it was captured and used by Nationalist squadrons and the German Condor Legion, which flew from here against Valencia and over the Ebro battle. It was abandoned after the war. Today the original command building houses the Centre d'Aviació Històrica de la Sénia, with aircraft displayed beside the flat former landing field.

catalonia-13.ev: Catalan Carlist volunteers attack towards Punta Targa from the Quatre Camins crossroads.
catalonia-13.rem: This small site is a reminder that Catalans fought on both sides of the battle.
catalonia-13.st: At the Quatre Camins crossroads south of Vilalba, the Catalan Carlist volunteers of the Tercio de Requetés de Nuestra Señora de Montserrat held a Nationalist position facing the Republican 31st Mixed Brigade on Punta Targa, only about 250 m away. On 19 August 1938 the requetés attacked and, by the unit's own figures, lost 58 killed and 174 wounded; Republican losses are not recorded. The site recalls that Catalans fought on both sides. Today a memorial cross stands at the crossroads.

catalonia-17.ev: Republican engineers keep the Móra d'Ebre crossings working under constant bombardment.

q.t: How did Republican engineers keep the crossings working?
o: By repairing and moving the pontoons night after night
By building a tunnel under the river
By using only ferries by day
q.x: Engineers repaired and moved the pontoon bridges night after night under bombardment.

catalonia-17.rem: Móra d'Ebre was the main supply artery of the Republican bridgehead.
catalonia-17.st: Móra d'Ebre, with its road bridge and the pontoon bridges thrown across the river after 25 July 1938, was the main supply artery of the Republican bridgehead and a constant target for Nationalist, German and Italian aircraft. Republican engineers kept the crossings working by repairing and moving the pontoons night after night. The hilltop castle served as a strongpoint and was left semi-ruined. Today the partly restored castle holds panels on the Ebro battle, with views of the river crossings.

catalonia-19.ev: The Camp de la Bóta becomes the main execution site of Francoist repression in Barcelona.
catalonia-19.rem: Most of those shot here are buried in the Fossar de la Pedrera; the Republican side also executed people here in 1936.
catalonia-19.st: The Camp de la Bóta, an old military ground on the shore at the edge of Barcelona, was the main execution site of Francoist repression in the city; it had also seen poorly documented Republican executions in 1936. Between 1939 and 1952 large numbers of people were shot here after court-martial, most of them buried in the Fossar de la Pedrera; counts differ between sources. Today Miquel Navarro's 'Fraternitat' sculpture stands near the Fòrum esplanade, and nothing of the camp survives.

catalonia-21.ev: George Orwell guards the POUM building from the Poliorama roof during the May Days.

q.t: What was Orwell guarding from the Poliorama roof?
q.x: On leave from the Aragon front, Orwell guarded the POUM executive building across the Rambla, as told in 'Homage to Catalonia'.

catalonia-21.rem: A month later the POUM was outlawed and Orwell escaped Spain as its members were arrested.
catalonia-21.st: George Orwell, on leave from the POUM militia on the Aragon front, spent the May Days of 1937 on the roof of the Poliorama cinema guarding the POUM executive building across the Rambla, as he describes in Homage to Catalonia. The centre of Barcelona was divided by barricades between CNT and POUM forces and those of the government and PSUC. A month later the POUM was outlawed, and Orwell escaped from Spain. Today the Poliorama's façade and clock tower look much as he knew them.

catalonia-22.ev: Revolutionary violence strikes priests, religious and Catholic laypeople; many churches burn.
catalonia-22.rem: The cathedral is a place to reflect on the violence against the Church in Barcelona in 1936.
catalonia-22.st: In the first months after the military rising was defeated in Barcelona in July 1936, a wave of revolutionary violence swept the Republican zone. Priests, monks, nuns and Catholic laypeople were among its main victims, and many churches were burned. Most killings were carried out by militia patrols and 'control committees' outside any legal process, until the authorities gradually reined them in. Some clergy killed then have since been beatified. Today the Gothic cathedral and its cloister offer a place for quiet reflection.

catalonia-24.ev: A shelter is dug beside the Serral farmhouse for the Republican airfield at Els Monjos.

q.t: What was the Serral farmhouse used for?
q.x: The shelter was dug next to the Serral farmhouse, which was used as a barracks for the airfield.

catalonia-24.rem: It is a rare surviving piece of the Republic's wartime air infrastructure in the Penedès.
catalonia-24.st: The Republican air force had a military airfield near Els Monjos in the Penedès, part of a network of Catalan fields that sheltered fighters and bombers from 1937. Because it made the area a bombing target, a shelter for about 120 people was dug in 1937 beside the Serral farmhouse, which served as a barracks. It is a rare surviving piece of the Republic's wartime air infrastructure. Today its brick-vaulted galleries and three ventilation shafts can be visited on a local memory route.

catalonia-25.ev: Republicans attack the Nationalist-fortified Mont de Conques in the failed May 1938 offensive.

q.t: Which rivers did the front settle along in western Catalonia?
q.x: After spring 1938 the front settled along the Segre and Noguera Pallaresa, with Nationalist bridgeheads at Tremp, Balaguer and Seròs.

catalonia-25.rem: The line held until the Nationalist Catalonia offensive of December 1938.
catalonia-25.st: After the Nationalist Aragon offensive of spring 1938, the front in western Catalonia settled along the Segre and Noguera Pallaresa rivers, with Nationalist bridgeheads at Tremp, Balaguer and Seròs. Mont de Conques, near Isona, was fortified by the Nationalists and attacked several times by the Republicans, especially in their costly and unsuccessful May 1938 offensive. The line held until the Nationalist Catalonia offensive of December 1938. Today Nationalist concrete positions and trenches remain, facing the Republican La Posa bunker across the valley.

catalonia-26.ev: President Azaña and other Republican leaders cross into France on foot by the Coll de Lli.
catalonia-26.rem: Thousands of refugees followed these same mountain paths into exile as Republican Catalonia fell.
catalonia-26.st: In the last days of the Republic in Catalonia, the border village of La Vajol sheltered members of the government and treasures evacuated from Barcelona, including paintings from the Prado. On 5 February 1939 Manuel Azaña, Diego Martínez Barrio, Lluís Companys and José Antonio Aguirre crossed into France on foot by the Coll de Lli, though accounts of their routes vary; thousands of refugees used the same paths. Today an exile monument and waymarked paths lead towards the border.

catalonia-27.ev: The dead of a Catalan Carlist unit that fought for the Nationalists are laid to rest here.
catalonia-27.rem: The crypt is a quiet reminder that Catalan society itself was divided by the war.
catalonia-27.st: The Tercio de Requetés de Nuestra Señora de Montserrat was a unit of Catalan Carlist volunteers who fought for the Nationalists, many of them having escaped from Republican Catalonia. It suffered heavy losses at Codo in August 1937 and in the Battle of the Ebro, and its dead were brought to a crypt at Montserrat, Catalonia's national shrine. The crypt recalls how deeply the war divided Catalan society. Today a mausoleum within the monastery complex records the names of the unit's dead.

catalonia-28.ev: Turned back at the border, the philosopher Walter Benjamin takes his own life in Portbou.
catalonia-28.rem: Portbou marks exile in both directions: Spaniards leaving in 1939, and refugees from Nazi-occupied France seeking escape in 1940.
catalonia-28.st: Portbou, the railway frontier town, was one of the main crossing points of the Retirada in February 1939. Eighteen months later refugees from Nazi-occupied France came the other way, and on 26 September 1940 the German-Jewish philosopher Walter Benjamin, turned back by the Spanish authorities after crossing the Pyrenees on foot, took his own life here. The place belongs to the story of exile rather than to the Civil War itself. Today Dani Karavan's steel stairway 'Passatges' descends towards the sea beside the cemetery.

catalonia-29.ev: Fearing invasion after 1944, the Franco regime builds the secret Línea P bunkers along the Pyrenees.

q.t: Why did the Franco regime build the Línea P bunkers?
o: To defend Barcelona against the 1938 offensive
Fearing an Allied or exile invasion after 1944
To shelter refugees crossing into France in 1939
q.x: The Línea P was built after the Republican guerrilla incursion into the Val d'Aran in October 1944. Its bunkers were never used in combat.

catalonia-29.rem: These are post-war works, showing how the regime's isolation and fears shaped the Pyrenean frontier.
catalonia-29.st: These bunkers belong to the war's aftermath rather than the war itself. After the Republican guerrilla incursion into the Val d'Aran in October 1944, the Franco regime, fearing an Allied or exile invasion, secretly built the 'Línea P', a chain of concrete bunkers from the Cap de Creus to the Basque coast that never saw combat. It shows how far post-war isolation and fear shaped the frontier. Today restored machine-gun and anti-tank bunkers, linking trenches and an interpretation centre form a park at Martinet.

north-01.ev: On market day, German and Italian aircraft bomb Gernika for about three hours, destroying the town centre.
north-01.rem: Gernika became the defining image of the bombing of civilians; the museum remembers it through survivors' voices and a message of reconciliation.
north-01.st: On the afternoon of Monday 26 April 1937, market day, aircraft of the German Condor Legion and the Italian Aviazione Legionaria bombed Gernika for about three hours in support of the Nationalist advance on Bilbao. Most of the town centre was destroyed; the death toll remains disputed. Reported by George Steer and painted by Picasso, the raid became the defining image of the bombing of civilians. Today the Peace Museum presents survivors' testimony and a section on reconciliation.

north-02.ev: The Assembly House and the oak of Gernika survive the bombing on the hill above the burning town.

q.t: Who posted a guard at the Tree of Gernika after the Nationalists took the town?
o: Carlist requetés of the Tercio de Begoña
Italian airmen of the Aviazione Legionaria
q.x: After the Nationalists took Gernika on 29 April 1937, Biscayan Carlist requetés of the Tercio de Begoña guarded the tree to stop it being damaged.

north-02.rem: The oak symbolises Basque self-government, which is one reason the town's destruction caused such outrage.
north-02.st: The Assembly House and the oak of Gernika were the historic symbols of Basque self-government, which deepened the outrage at the town's destruction in April 1937. Both survived the bombing on the hill above the burning centre. After the Nationalists took Gernika on 29 April, Carlist requetés of the Tercio de Begoña, themselves Biscayans, posted a guard to protect the tree. Today the preserved old trunk stands under a colonnade beside the living oak.

north-03.ev: Basque and Republican units make a final defence of Bilbao on Artxanda while civilians evacuate westwards.

q.t: What does the large 'fingerprint' sculpture on Artxanda honour?
o: All those who died in the war
The Nationalist troops who entered Bilbao
q.x: Juan José Novella's Huella Dactilar sculpture honours all those who died in the war, near a restored stretch of trench.

north-03.rem: Artxanda was the last defended position before Bilbao fell to Nationalist troops on 19 June 1937.
north-03.st: Mount Artxanda, above Bilbao, was the last defended position before the city fell. After the Nationalists broke through the Iron Belt at Gaztelumendi on 12 June 1937, Basque and Republican units fell back here for a final, bitter defence while civilians were evacuated westwards. The Basque Army withdrew on 18 June and Nationalist troops entered Bilbao the next day. Today a restored trench, Juan José Novella's fingerprint memorial to all who died in the war and a panoramic view over Bilbao await the visitor.

north-04.ev: Italian bombers strike Durango during morning Mass, killing priests, nuns and worshippers.
north-04.rem: Bombed almost four weeks before Gernika, Durango is often remembered as its forgotten precursor.
north-04.st: On 31 March 1937, the first day of General Mola's offensive against Biscay, Italian Savoia-Marchetti S.81 bombers with German and Italian escorts attacked Durango, a road and rail junction behind the front. The first wave struck during morning Mass, killing priests, nuns and worshippers at the Jesuit church and the Santa Susana convent. Bombed almost four weeks before Gernika, Durango is often called its forgotten precursor. Today the Uribarri basilica stands on a route of memorial plaques.

north-05.ev: Basque and Republican battalions hold the Intxorta heights through the winter until the front collapses.

q.t: When did the defenders finally have to abandon the Intxorta line?
o: In September 1936, soon after most of Gipuzkoa fell
In June 1937, after the fall of Bilbao
In late April 1937, as the front collapsed
q.x: The battalions held Intxorta through the winter and the first weeks of Mola's 1937 offensive, abandoning it in late April 1937.

north-05.rem: Intxorta became a symbol of Basque resistance; the Elgeta centre also tells the story of recovering its memory.
north-05.st: After most of Gipuzkoa was lost in 1936, Basque and Republican battalions stabilised the front on the Intxorta heights above Elgeta. They held these trenches through the winter and the first weeks of Mola's spring offensive, until the line was abandoned in late April 1937 as the front collapsed towards Durango and Bilbao. Intxorta became a symbol of Basque resistance. Today an interpretation centre in Elgeta and a waymarked loop lead to restored trenches, shelters, viewpoints and the Intxortako Atea monument.

north-06.ev: Beneath the Plaza del Príncipe, a shelter is dug for commanders and officials as raids hit Santander.

q.t: How was this shelter rediscovered?
o: It was exposed by the great fire of 1941
By Italian troops searching the city in 1937
During works on the Plaza Porticada in 2006
q.x: Abandoned after the war and buried in the rebuilding after the 1941 fire, the shelter was rediscovered in 2006 and opened as a museum in 2014.

north-06.rem: Over a hundred shelters were dug beneath Republican Santander during the bombing of 1937.
north-06.st: Santander, then in the Republican zone, was bombed repeatedly during 1937, and over a hundred shelters were dug beneath the city. This one, under the Plaza del Príncipe, was built in spring 1937 for about 70 people, mainly military commanders and city officials. Buried after the great fire of 1941, it was rediscovered in 2006 and opened as a museum in 2014. Today restored galleries display period photographs, an airman's equipment and a bomb.

north-07.ev: Outnumbered Republican troops hold the El Mazuco pass and Sierra del Cuera against Navarrese brigades.

q.t: Why did the Condor Legion's carpet-bombing have limited effect here?
o: The Republicans had strong anti-aircraft guns
The rugged terrain blunted its effect
q.x: The Condor Legion tried some of its first carpet-bombing tactics at El Mazuco, but the rugged limestone terrain blunted their effect.

north-07.rem: Peña Turbina, the range's highest point, was the last main Republican position; its fall on 22 September opened eastern Asturias.
north-07.st: After Santander fell, the Nationalists pushed west into Asturias. At the El Mazuco pass and on the Sierra del Cuera, about 5,000 Republican troops of the XIV Army Corps, many of them CNT militia, held off far stronger Navarrese brigades under José Solchaga, backed by the Condor Legion and Italian units. Peña Turbina, the last main Republican position, fell on 22 September 1937, opening eastern Asturias. Today hiking routes cross the former front line.

north-08.ev: Market crowds and refugees shelter in these hillside tunnels as bombs fall on Gernika.

q.t: How many of Gernika's four tunnel shelters survive?
q.x: Gernika dug four tunnel shelters in 1936; two survive, one with a scale model and one with a sound-and-light presentation.
