north-08.rem: These tunnels were in use during the raid of 26 April 1937, sheltering townspeople and refugees from the market.
north-08.st: In 1936 Gernika dug four tunnel shelters into the hillside by the market area to protect its people from air raids. On 26 April 1937 crowds from the Monday market and refugees sheltered here as the bombs fell on the town. Two of the four shelters survive, a short and quiet complement to the Peace Museum. Today one tunnel holds a scale model of the shelter as built, and the other a sound-and-light presentation recalling the experience of the people inside during the raid.

north-09.ev: Massed artillery and aircraft break through Bilbao's Iron Belt at its weak Gaztelumendi sector.

q.t: What helped reveal the Iron Belt's weak points to the Nationalists?
o: Aerial photographs taken by the Condor Legion
Its engineer defected with the plans
q.x: Engineer Alejandro Goicoechea defected to the Nationalists with the Iron Belt's plans. On 12 June 1937 the attack broke through at Gaztelumendi.

north-09.rem: Held by far fewer defenders than planned, the Iron Belt failed, and Bilbao fell a week after the breach.
north-09.st: The Iron Belt ringed Bilbao with trenches, bunkers and gun positions, but it was held by far fewer men than planned, and the engineer Alejandro Goicoechea defected to the Nationalists with its plans. On 12 June 1937 the Nationalists concentrated heavy artillery and more than a hundred aircraft on the weak Gaztelumendi sector at Larrabetzu and broke through; Bilbao fell a week later. Today a bunker built into a farmhouse near Sarrikola marks the breach sector.

north-10.ev: Fighting spreads along the ridge above Zamudio as Nationalists cross the Iron Belt and descend.

q.t: What can walkers see along the Zamudio memory trail?
o: A rebuilt castle and war museum
q.x: The waymarked trail climbs to the Berreaga–Gaztelumendi ridge past original trenches and concrete machine-gun posts.

north-10.rem: Here you can see what the Iron Belt looked like on the ground, and why it failed against massed artillery and aircraft.
north-10.st: Zamudio lies directly below the stretch of the Iron Belt where the Nationalists broke through. The fighting of 11–13 June 1937 spread along the Berreaga–Urrusti–Gaztelumendi ridge, and on 12 June the attackers crossed the line and came down into the village. The ridge shows clearly what the Iron Belt looked like on the ground and why it failed against massed artillery and aircraft. Today a signposted memory trail climbs past original trenches and concrete machine-gun posts, with explanatory panels along the way.

north-11.ev: Two light bombers attack the crowded Andikona square during the Santa Marina fiestas.
north-11.rem: Most of those killed here were civilians, many of them children; a sculpture in the square honours them.
north-11.st: On 22 July 1936, four days after the coup, two Breguet XIX light bombers flown by Ángel Salas Larrazábal and José Muñoz Jiménez bombed and machine-gunned the Andikona square in Otxandio, crowded for the Santa Marina fiestas. Most of those killed were civilians, many of them children. Often called 'the first Gernika', it was one of the war's first air attacks to kill a crowd of civilians. Today a memorial sculpture in the square honours the victims.

north-12.ev: Navarrese columns attack Irun and take San Marcial hill, cutting the Republican north off from France.

q.t: Why did the defenders of Irun run short of ammunition?
o: Rival units refused to share supplies
q.x: With the French border closed, the Basque, CNT and Asturian defenders ran short of ammunition. San Marcial fell and Irun was abandoned on 5 September.

north-12.rem: The Nationalist victory at Irun cut Gipuzkoa, Biscay, Santander and Asturias off from the French border.
north-12.st: Mola's Navarrese columns under Colonel Alfonso Beorlegui, supported by German and Italian aircraft, attacked Irun to cut the Republican north off from France. Basque militia, CNT units, Asturian miners and some French communist volunteers held the Puntza ridge and San Marcial, but with the border closed they ran short of ammunition, and Irun was abandoned on 5 September 1936. Today the hilltop hermitage offers a wide view over the battlefield, Irun, Hendaye and the Bidasoa.

north-13.ev: Italian CTV divisions attack and take the Escudo pass, opening the road to Santander.
north-13.rem: The pyramid is a Fascist-era memorial to Italian dead; its future is debated under Spain's democratic memory legislation.
north-13.st: The Escudo pass carries the main road from Burgos to Santander over the Cantabrian range. When the Nationalist offensive on Santander opened on 14 August 1937, Italian CTV divisions attacked here and took the pass by 17 August, encircling Republican units; Santander fell on 26 August. The memorial to the Italian dead is a Fascist-era monument whose future is debated. Today a stone pyramid stands beside the N-623 at the summit, with wide mountain views.

north-14.ev: Colonel Aranda holds Oviedo for the rising while Asturian miners' militias besiege the city.

q.t: How did Colonel Aranda secure Oviedo for the rising?
o: He had persuaded Republican leaders he was loyal
He arrived by sea with Galician troops
He negotiated a truce with the miners
q.x: Aranda had persuaded Republican leaders of his loyalty, then declared for the rising on 19 July 1936 and held the city through a long siege.

north-14.rem: Oviedo survived months of siege until a column from Galicia opened a corridor in October 1936; its old centre was heavily damaged.
north-14.st: On 19 July 1936 Colonel Antonio Aranda, who had persuaded Republican leaders he was loyal, declared for the rising and held Oviedo with soldiers, Civil Guards and Falangist volunteers. Surrounded by Asturian miners' militias, the city endured months of siege and street fighting until a Nationalist column from Galicia opened a corridor in October 1936. Today the town hall on Plaza de la Constitución faces San Isidoro church in an old quarter largely rebuilt after the siege.

north-15.ev: Many of those executed after Asturias falls are shot at the cemetery walls and buried here.
north-15.rem: The names of identified victims are engraved around the common grave, one of the largest memorials of its kind in northern Spain.
north-15.st: After Asturias fell in October 1937, Francoist courts-martial and extrajudicial killings claimed many lives, with about 1,000 executions in Oviedo alone. Many of those shot against the walls of El Salvador cemetery were buried in a common grave here. Earlier, in the Republican zone, rightists and clergy had also been killed in Asturias in 1934 and 1936. Today memorial walls around the grave bear the names of 1,316 identified victims; the full toll is still being researched.

north-16.ev: Italian-Spanish and Navarrese brigades attack Sollube, the height commanding the coast road to Bilbao.

q.t: Why was losing Sollube so serious for Bilbao's defenders?
o: It held the city's main arms factory
It cut the railway line to Santander
It opened the coastal approach to the Iron Belt
q.x: Sollube commands the Bermeo–Bilbao coast road; its loss opened the coastal approach to the Iron Belt and was seen as the beginning of the end.

north-16.rem: Both sides suffered heavy losses on Sollube, whose fall marked the beginning of the end of Bilbao's defence.
north-16.st: Sollube commands the coast road between Bermeo and Bilbao. In May 1937 it was attacked by the Italian-Spanish Flechas Negras brigade under Sandro Piazzoni and the IV Navarrese Brigade, and defended by Basque, Asturian and Cantabrian battalions. The mountain fell around 8 May after heavy losses on both sides, opening the coastal approach to Bilbao's Iron Belt. Today it is an open mountain with wide views to Bermeo and the Urdaibai estuary; any remains are unsigned.

north-17.ev: Nationalist defenders ring Oviedo with concrete positions facing Republican lines on Monte Naranco.

q.t: Which side built the concrete bunker at Cerdeño?
q.x: After the Galician column reached Oviedo in October 1936, the Nationalist defenders ringed the city with concrete positions like this one.

north-17.rem: These positions stayed on a front line until Asturias fell in October 1937.
north-17.st: Once the Galician relief column reached Oviedo in October 1936, the Nationalist defenders ringed the city with concrete positions facing Republican lines on Monte Naranco and in the surrounding villages. These works stayed on a front line until Asturias fell in October 1937, and the Naranco slopes above were fought over repeatedly. Archaeologists have since mapped many of the trenches and bunkers. Today a surviving Nationalist bunker stands at Cerdeño, on the city's northern outskirts.

north-18.ev: Colonel Pinilla's garrison holds the Simancas barracks under siege until militias storm it in August.

q.t: What did Colonel Pinilla do as the barracks were stormed?
o: He surrendered to the Asturian militias
He escaped by sea to the cruiser
He radioed the cruiser to fire on his own position
q.x: As the militias stormed the barracks in mid-August 1936, Pinilla radioed the Almirante Cervera to fire on his position. Almost the entire garrison died.

north-18.rem: The Franco regime made the siege a heroic legend; its memorial is now a contested symbol under democratic memory law.
north-18.st: When the coup failed in Gijón, Colonel Antonio Pinilla and about 600 soldiers of the Simancas regiment shut themselves into the Simancas barracks. Asturian militias besieged them, and when the building was stormed in mid-August 1936, Pinilla radioed the cruiser Almirante Cervera to fire on his own position; almost the entire garrison died. The Franco regime turned the siege into a heroic legend. Today the 1958 Francoist monument on the site faces removal orders and may be gone or covered.

north-19.ev: After Gijón falls, Republicans executed at the Ceares cemetery wall are buried in a common grave.
north-19.rem: Families and memory associations gather here each year to remember those buried in the common grave.
north-19.st: After Gijón fell on 21 October 1937, ending the war in the North, thousands of Republicans were imprisoned and many were tried by courts-martial and shot. Those executed at the wall of the Ceares municipal cemetery were buried in a common grave, recorded as holding 1,293 victims of the war and the years that followed. Today a memorial area marks the grave, a place of annual remembrance for families and memory associations.

north-20.ev: The Astra arms factory builds two disguised concrete shelters for its workers in Gernika.

q.t: Why did the bombers not recognise the factory's shelters?
o: They were disguised under false roofs
They were dug deep inside a mountain
They were painted to look like a church
q.x: Built in September 1936, the two shelters were disguised under false roofs. The factory buildings largely survived the raid of 26 April 1937.

north-20.rem: The survival of the arms factories is often cited in the debate over what the Gernika raid was really aiming at.
north-20.st: Gernika's arms industry, which made the Astra pistols, was one of the few potentially military targets in the town. In September 1936 the factory built two concrete shelters for its workers, disguised under false roofs, which the bombers did not recognise on 26 April 1937. The factory buildings largely survived the raid, a fact often cited in the debate over what the attack was really aiming at. Today a shelter remains on Ibarra Kalea.

north-21.ev: The western end of Bilbao's Iron Belt runs through the Uribe district to the coast.

q.t: Where did the Iron Belt's western end reach the coast?
q.x: The line ran through the Uribe district north of Bilbao to the coast at Barrika and Sopela, where remains are marked by panels.

north-21.rem: The Berango centre explains how the Iron Belt was built and why it failed in June 1937.
north-21.st: The western end of Bilbao's Iron Belt ran through the Uribe district north of the city to the coast at Barrika and Sopela. Remains of bunkers, trenches and gun emplacements survive in several municipalities, among them Berango, Urduliz, Gatika, Loiu, Mungia and Zamudio, and together they show how the line was built and why it failed in June 1937. Today the small interpretation centre in Berango displays panels, objects and documents, and makes a good starting point for walks to the signposted remains.

south-01.ev: Almería digs more than 4 km of shelter galleries to protect civilians from repeated air and sea attacks.

q.t: What was the worst single attack on Almería?
o: A Condor Legion raid on the harbour in 1938
A German naval bombardment at dawn on 31 May 1937
An air raid during the arrival of Málaga's refugees
q.x: The cruiser Admiral Scheer and four destroyers shelled the city in reprisal for a Republican air attack on the cruiser Deutschland off Ibiza.

south-01.rem: The galleries, with their own operating theatre, form one of Europe's largest civilian shelter networks.
south-01.st: Almería, the Republic's main port on the south-east coast, was bombed repeatedly from the air and the sea. At dawn on 31 May 1937 the German cruiser Admiral Scheer and four destroyers shelled the city in reprisal for a Republican air attack on the Deutschland off Ibiza, killing civilians. The city dug one of Europe's largest civilian shelter networks, more than 4 km of galleries. Today about 1 km of restored galleries includes an underground operating theatre.

south-02.ev: Republican supporters, trade unionists and teachers are taken from Víznar at night and shot in this ravine.
south-02.rem: For many, this ravine stands for all the victims of the repression in Granada; the full number buried here is still unknown.
south-02.st: After the military rising took Granada in July 1936, the rebel civil government organised the execution of Republican supporters, trade unionists, teachers and politicians. Many were taken at night from La Colonia, a house in Víznar, and shot in this pine-covered ravine, where they were buried in pits and hollows; the total number buried here is unknown. Today a path through the pines leads to marked graves, the monolith 'Todos eran Lorca' and plaques bearing victims' names.

south-03.ev: Federico García Lorca and three other men are shot near the Fuente Grande spring by rebel authorities.
south-03.rem: The park honours Lorca and all victims of the war; the place where he lies has never been found.
south-03.st: Federico García Lorca, Spain's best-known poet and dramatist, was arrested in Granada on 16 August 1936 and shot days later near the Fuente Grande spring, with the schoolteacher Dióscoro Galindo and the banderilleros Francisco Galadí and Joaquín Arcollas. His killing by the rebel authorities became a worldwide symbol of the war's repression. A 2009 excavation at the supposed grave found nothing, and his resting place remains unknown. Today the park holds fountains, walls bearing his verse and an old olive tree.

south-04.ev: Lorca returns to his family's summer home just before the rising; the house is later searched.

q.t: Where did Lorca take refuge after the military seized Granada?
o: In the house of the Rosales family
q.x: Lorca sheltered with the Rosales family, Falangists and friends, but was arrested there on 16 August 1936 and killed days later near Alfacar.

south-04.rem: Here Lorca wrote much of Blood Wedding and Yerma; it is the place to meet the writer before visiting the sites of his death.
south-04.st: This was the García Lorca family's summer home from 1926 to 1936, where the poet wrote much of Blood Wedding and Yerma. When the military seized Granada the house was searched, and his brother-in-law Manuel Fernández-Montesinos, the Socialist mayor, was arrested and shot. Lorca took refuge with the Rosales family, Falangists and friends, but was arrested there on 16 August 1936 and killed days later near Alfacar. Today the whitewashed farmhouse, largely unchanged, keeps family furniture, his desk and piano, drawings and documents.

south-05.ev: Civilians and militiamen fleeing Málaga set out along the coast road towards Almería under attack.
south-05.rem: This walk honours those who fled, and Norman Bethune and the Canadian aid that carried the weakest to safety.
south-05.st: When Nationalist and Italian CTV forces took Málaga on 8 February 1937, a huge column of civilians and militiamen fled east along the coast road towards Almería. They were shelled from the sea and attacked from the air, and many died of exhaustion or drowned at river crossings; the death toll is unknown. The Canadian surgeon Norman Bethune and his companions ferried the weakest to Almería. Today a seafront walk at the Peñón del Cuervo cove carries a plaque to Bethune.

south-06.ev: Civil Guards and civilians hold this hilltop sanctuary for over seven months inside Republican territory.

q.t: How were the besieged defenders of the sanctuary supplied?
o: By Nationalist aircraft dropping food and medicine
By a relief column from Lopera
q.x: Nationalist aircraft dropped food and medicine for more than seven months. Republican forces stormed the ruins on 1 May 1937 and the survivors surrendered.

south-06.rem: The Franco regime made the siege a heroic legend; the monument's narrative is debated under democratic memory law.
south-06.st: In September 1936 about 250 Civil Guards, some Falangists and around 1,000 family members and civilians shut themselves into this hilltop sanctuary, deep in Republican territory. Captain Santiago Cortés held out for more than seven months, supplied by Nationalist air drops, until Republican forces stormed the ruins on 1 May 1937; Cortés was mortally wounded and the survivors surrendered. Franco's regime made the siege a heroic legend. Today the rebuilt sanctuary stands beside a 1965 monument whose Francoist narrative is debated.

south-07.ev: The newly formed XIV International Brigade attacks the hills around Lopera and is beaten back.
south-07.rem: Lopera was the International Brigades' last action in Andalusia; the front then stayed here until 1939.
south-07.st: On Christmas Day 1936 Nationalist troops took Lopera during their 'olive offensive' towards Andújar. The newly formed XIV International Brigade under General 'Walter', volunteers with little training and scant support, attacked the hills and was beaten off by requetés and Moroccan Regulares; the poet John Cornford and the novelist Ralph Fox were among the English-speaking company's dead. Today the Jardín de los Poetas Ingleses holds a relief of Cornford, and machine-gun nests survive outside town.

south-08.ev: Refugees fleeing Málaga along the coast road meet those coming down from the Axarquía villages here.
south-08.rem: Almond trees flower here each February beside plaques bearing survivors' names in their own handwriting.
south-08.st: Torre del Mar, about 30 km east of Málaga, was where refugees fleeing along the coast road met those coming down from the villages of the Axarquía in February 1937. In 2007 the town opened this memorial garden, conceived as a place to meet rather than a monument, and the annual commemoration of the Desbandá is held here. Today a cracked 'MÁLAGA 1937 / NUNCA MÁS' plaque, almond trees and hundreds of handwritten survivors' plaques fill the garden.

south-09.ev: Republican supporters killed by military courts and summary shootings are buried in mass graves here.
south-09.rem: The recovered remains now rest in the memorial pantheon; Málaga's two waves of killing should be understood together.
south-09.st: After Málaga fell in February 1937, military courts and summary shootings killed many Republican supporters, often against the wall of the old San Rafael cemetery, and their bodies were placed in mass graves. Between 2006 and 2009 archaeologists exhumed 2,840 bodies here. Málaga had also seen heavy repression in the Republican zone before the city fell, and the two waves should be understood together. Today a park holds the Panteón de la Memoria, with the recovered remains, and walls of names.

south-10.ev: Victims of the repression after Queipo de Llano seizes Seville are buried in this mass grave.
south-10.rem: Pico Reja holds many victims of the repression in Seville; excavation and identification continue here.
south-10.st: General Gonzalo Queipo de Llano seized Seville on 18 July 1936, crushing working-class resistance in Triana and La Macarena and threatening opponents with death in nightly radio speeches. Many victims of the repression that followed were buried in Pico Reja, a mass grave in San Fernando cemetery, probably including Blas Infante, the 'father of Andalusian nationalism', though his remains have not been confirmed. Today the cemetery holds the excavated Pico Reja area and memorial markers; the site may be fenced.

south-11.ev: Villanueva de Córdoba builds an underground shelter beneath its main square as Nationalist aircraft bomb the area.

q.t: Where was Queipo de Llano's 1937 push towards the Almadén mines stopped?
q.x: In March–April 1937 Republican forces stopped the offensive at Pozoblanco, and the front stayed close by until the end of the war.

south-11.rem: The shelter is one of Andalusia's declared Places of Democratic Memory.
south-11.st: Villanueva de Córdoba lay in the Republican-held north of Córdoba province, close to the front around Pozoblanco. In spring 1937 Queipo de Llano's forces tried to break through to the Almadén mercury mines and were stopped at Pozoblanco, and the front stayed close by until the end of the war. As Nationalist aircraft bombed the towns of the area, Villanueva built an underground shelter in 1937. Today that shelter lies beneath the Plaza de España.

south-12.ev: Robert Capa's 'Falling Soldier' photograph has been matched to the skyline around Espejo.

q.t: How was the 'Falling Soldier' photograph linked to Espejo?
o: A local farmer recognised the militiaman
Capa's own notebook named the village
Its skyline was matched to Espejo's outskirts
q.x: In 2009 José Manuel Susperregui matched the skyline to Espejo, where the front was quiet. The place, the man and whether it was staged remain disputed.

south-12.rem: The war's most famous photograph remains disputed; Espejo shows how the first summer's front ran through open countryside.
south-12.st: Robert Capa's photograph of a militiaman falling backwards, published in Vu in September 1936, became the defining image of the war. For decades it was said to show the anarchist Federico Borrell García killed at Cerro Muriano, but in 2009 José Manuel Susperregui matched the skyline to the outskirts of Espejo, where the front was then quiet; the location, the soldier's identity and whether the scene was staged all remain disputed. Today open, rolling farmland surrounds Espejo, with no known memorial or marker.

south-13.ev: Refugees fleeing Málaga cross this bridge as the coast road nearby is shelled from the sea.
south-13.rem: Many were killed on this stretch of road; the bridge is now a Place of Democratic Memory.
south-13.st: The old bridge over the Barranco de Maro, east of Nerja, carried the coast road used by refugees fleeing Málaga in February 1937. Nearby the road was shelled from the sea, many were killed at the Río de la Miel crossing, and in Nerja evacuation buses carrying children were bombed. How many died on this stretch is unknown. Today the old stone bridge still spans the ravine on the old coast road, with a memorial plaque.

south-14.ev: Refugees from Málaga arrive at Almería's harbour, which German warships bombard in May.
south-14.rem: The Almadrabillas memorial remembers Andalusian Republican exiles deported to Mauthausen, many of whom never returned.
south-14.st: Almería's harbour received tens of thousands of refugees from Málaga in February 1937 and was the target of the German naval bombardment of 31 May 1937. After the war, many Andalusian Republican exiles who had fled to France were captured by the Germans in 1940 and deported to Mauthausen, where many of them did not survive; their numbers vary between sources. Today the harbour front and a memorial in the Parque de las Almadrabillas, beside the port, remember the deportees.

south-15.ev: A Republican guerrilla unit lands by boat and frees prisoners held as forced labourers at Carchuna.
south-15.rem: Prisoners, mostly Asturian miners, were held here as forced labourers until the raid brought many of them to freedom.
south-15.st: After the fall of Málaga the front on the Granada coast stabilised near Motril and stayed there until 1939. On 23 May 1938 a Republican guerrilla unit landed by boat and attacked the fort of Carchuna, where prisoners, mostly Asturian miners, were held as forced labourers, and many of them escaped to the Republican lines. It was one of the most successful special operations of the war. Today the 18th-century coastal fort and remains of front-line trenches survive.

south-16.ev: German and Italian transports fly Franco's Army of Africa from Tetuán to Seville in the first large airlift.

q.t: Why was Franco's Army of Africa flown to Spain rather than shipped?
o: There were no ships left in Morocco
The Republican navy was blocking the Strait
Storms had closed the Moroccan ports
q.x: With the Republican navy blocking the Strait, transports flew legionnaires and Regulares to Tablada and Jerez; the troops then marched north.

south-16.rem: This was the first large military airlift in history, and it carried the Army of Africa towards Badajoz and Madrid.
south-16.st: With the Republican navy blocking the Strait, Franco's Army of Africa was stuck in Morocco. From late July 1936 German Junkers Ju 52 and Italian Savoia-Marchetti transports flew legionnaires and Regulares from Tetuán to Seville, landing mainly at Tablada and at Jerez, in the first large military airlift in history. The troops then marched north towards Badajoz and Madrid, and the airfield later served as a military base and aviation school. Today Tablada remains a military base, and only its perimeter can be seen.

levant-01.ev: After a four-hour Condor Legion raid, Cartagena begins tunnelling shelters like this one into its hills.

q.t: Why was Cartagena one of the most heavily bombed cities of the war?
o: It was the Republic's main naval base
It was the seat of the Republican government
It was the Nationalists' main supply port
q.x: As home of the Republican fleet, Cartagena was bombed heavily. This gallery, for more than 5,000 people, was unfinished when the city fell in 1939.

levant-01.rem: The museum shows daily life under the bombs and how the city defended itself against air attack.
levant-01.st: Cartagena, the Republic's main naval base, was one of the most heavily bombed cities of the war. After a four-hour Condor Legion raid on 25 November 1936, the city began tunnelling shelters into its hills; this gallery in the Cerro de la Concepción, designed for more than 5,000 people, was still unfinished when Cartagena fell on 31 March 1939. Today the tunnel holds exhibition rooms, photographs, sirens and audiovisuals, with a panoramic lift rising to the castle.

levant-02.ev: Architect José Luis Testor builds a shelter for 700 children beside Valencia's Town Hall.

q.t: Who was the shelter under the Casa de la Enseñanza built for?
q.x: Built in 1938 by José Luis Testor, the school shelter had five vaulted chambers for 700 children, with ventilation, lighting and latrines.

levant-02.rem: As seat of the Republican government, Valencia became a target; it dug more than 50 public shelters against the raids.
levant-02.st: From November 1936 to October 1937 Valencia was the seat of the Republican government, and it became a target; Italian bombers from Mallorca carried out most of the raids. The city dug more than 50 public shelters, and in 1938 the architect José Luis Testor built this school shelter beside the Town Hall for 700 children. Today five barrel-vaulted concrete chambers keep their original benches and restored signage, with panels on the bombing of Valencia.

levant-04.ev: Italian bombers from Mallorca strike Alicante's crowded morning market before the sirens sound.
levant-04.rem: Each day at noon nine plaques glow red for ten minutes, one for each aircraft, in memory of those killed at the market.
levant-04.st: At 11:18 on 25 May 1938, Italian Aviazione Legionaria SM.79 bombers from Mallorca dropped about 90 bombs on central Alicante while the morning market was crowded and before the sirens had sounded. It was one of the deadliest raids of the war on a purely civilian target, and the death toll differs between records. Today nine plaques in the square, one for each aircraft, glow red at noon, and a siren and a stopped clock are kept inside the market.

levant-05.ev: Tens of thousands of Republicans crowd Alicante's quays hoping for evacuation as the Republic collapses.

q.t: What was the Stanbrook?
o: A British collier that carried refugees to Oran
A Republican warship that escaped to Bizerte
An Italian transport bringing troops to the port
q.x: Under Captain Archibald Dickson, the collier Stanbrook sailed for Oran on 28 March 1939, far beyond capacity; very few ships came after her.

levant-05.rem: Thousands left on the quays were taken prisoner; the Valencian government now marks 28 March as a day of remembrance.
levant-05.st: As the Republic collapsed in March 1939, tens of thousands of Republican soldiers, officials and families converged on Alicante hoping for evacuation by sea. On 28 March the British collier Stanbrook, under Captain Archibald Dickson, sailed for Oran far beyond her capacity, but very few ships followed and many thousands were left on the quays. After the port was taken, they were marched to Los Almendros and Albatera. Today a plaque to the Stanbrook's crew stands on the quayside.

levant-08.ev: Nationalist and Italian forces attack the Línea XYZ and break against it short of Valencia.

q.t: Who held the Línea XYZ against the July 1938 attacks?
q.x: Under General Menéndez, the Ejército de Levante held the line less than 40 km from Valencia. Days later the Republic launched the Ebro offensive.

levant-08.rem: The trenches of La Muela and La Vegatilla, part of the rear line, are among the best-preserved of the Línea XYZ.
levant-08.st: After reaching the sea at Vinaròs in April 1938, Franco turned south towards Valencia, and the Republic dug the Línea XYZ, a system of trenches, shelters and bunkers about 150 km long. In July 1938 the forces of Varela, García Valiño, Solchaga and the Italian CTV attacked it and broke against it less than 40 km from Valencia, as the Ejército de Levante held. Today well-preserved trenches, parapets and machine-gun nests survive around La Muela and the Alto de Sayas.

levant-11.ev: The Franco regime uses this quarry wall beside Paterna cemetery as the province's main execution site.
levant-11.rem: Those shot here lie in the neighbouring cemetery, where the 2238 memorial records their names; relatives, many of them women, drove the exhumations.
levant-11.st: After Valencia fell in March 1939, the Franco regime used the wall of a former quarry beside Paterna cemetery, known as the 'Paredón de España', as its main execution site in the province. Records document 2,238 people shot here between 1939 and 1956 and buried in mass graves in the neighbouring cemetery. Exhumations have been driven largely by victims' relatives. Today the bullet-scarred wall carries a monument and plaques, and the cemetery holds the '2238' memorial listing the names.

levant-03.ev: The Republican government, having left Madrid, runs its Presidency from this Borja palace in Valencia.

q.t: Why did the Republican government move to Valencia in November 1936?
o: Valencia had better rail links to France
The Cortes voted to abolish Madrid as capital
q.x: With Madrid seemingly about to fall, Largo Caballero's government moved to Valencia, which remained the capital until autumn 1937.

levant-03.rem: Here the Republic reorganised its army and weathered the crisis of May 1937, when Negrín replaced Largo Caballero.
levant-03.st: When Madrid seemed about to fall in November 1936, Francisco Largo Caballero's government left for Valencia, which remained the Republic's capital until autumn 1937. This 15th-century Borja palace housed the Presidency of the government, and here the Republic reorganised its army and passed through the crisis of May 1937, when Juan Negrín replaced Largo Caballero. Today the Gothic–Renaissance palace, seat of the Valencian parliament, faces Plaza de San Lorenzo; there is no Civil War display.

levant-06.ev: Prisoners taken at Alicante port are held in an open almond grove with almost no food or water.
levant-06.rem: No original structures survive; a quiet monolith in the park recalls those held here, and those taken away and shot.
levant-06.st: Prisoners taken at Alicante port were held from 31 March 1939 in an almond grove at La Goteta, an open field ringed with barbed wire, with almost no food or water. For about a week many thousands were held here before most were moved to Albatera or to prisons, and some were taken out and shot; there are no reliable records of how many died. Today a small memorial monolith stands in a neighbourhood park on the site; no original structures survive.

levant-07.ev: Alicante shelters its people beneath its squares as Italian aircraft from Mallorca bomb the city.

q.t: Which other Alicante shelter does the city open alongside Plaza Séneca?
q.x: Plaza Séneca and Plaza Balmis are the two shelters Alicante opens as memory sites, with soundscapes recreating a raid.

levant-07.rem: The deadliest raid on Alicante came on 25 May 1938; this shelter lets visitors imagine the sirens and the bombs.
levant-07.st: Alicante, a Republican port and supply base, was bombed repeatedly by Italian aircraft from Mallorca, most deadly on 25 May 1938. The city responded with public shelters under its squares, and the Plaza Séneca shelter is one of two that the city now opens as a memory site. A linked exhibition tells the story of the city's war and its end in the port. Today restored underground galleries host a sound-and-light installation recreating an air raid.

levant-09.ev: Repeated Nationalist frontal assaults along the Teruel–Sagunto road fail against Republican positions around Viver.

q.t: How did Republican engineers build the defences at Viver?
o: Using the broken terrain for a network of positions
q.x: Engineers used the broken terrain to build trenches, shelters and bunkers covering the road and the El Ragudo railway pass.

levant-09.rem: Despite more men and command of the air, the Nationalists could not break through at Viver, the centre of the Línea XYZ.
levant-09.st: Viver lay at the centre of the Línea XYZ, where the Nationalist drive down the Teruel–Sagunto road and railway was stopped in July 1938. Republican engineers used the broken terrain rather than a continuous wall, covering the road and the railway pass at El Ragudo with trenches, shelters and bunkers. Although the Nationalists had more men and command of the air, repeated frontal assaults here failed. Today signposted walks lead to the Morredondo trenches, Cerro Cruz and El Ragudo.

levant-12.ev: Built by the Republic as a labour camp, Albatera becomes a Francoist concentration camp in 1939.
levant-12.rem: Prisoners from both sides of the war were held here; in 1939 hunger, disease and executions took many lives.
levant-12.st: The Republic built this camp near San Isidro in 1937 as a labour camp, where around 1,000 prisoners, many suspected of Nationalist sympathies, drained the Saladares marshes. After April 1939 the victors turned it into a concentration camp for Republicans taken at Alicante; hunger, lice and disease killed many, and prisoners were removed for execution. The number held is uncertain because the records were destroyed. Today a 1995 memorial of iron beams and chains stands near the station.

levant-13.ev: Coastal guns near Cabo Tiñoso sink the Nationalist transport Castillo de Olite approaching Cartagena.
levant-13.rem: Castillitos' two 381 mm guns remain in place, built to guard the Republic's main naval base.
levant-13.st: Castillitos, built between 1933 and 1936 in a mock-castle style, mounted two Vickers 381 mm guns guarding Cartagena and is reported to have fired only once in the war. The Cabo Tiñoso batteries mattered at the very end: in March 1939 troops loyal to the Republic retook them, and on 7 March a shell from the neighbouring La Parajola battery hit the Nationalist transport Castillo de Olite, where 1,476 of 2,112 men died. Today both barrels remain in their clifftop emplacements.

levant-14.ev: Castelló builds a public shelter under Plaza Tetuán as raids increase before the city falls.

q.t: When did Castelló fall to Nationalist troops?
q.x: Castelló was bombed as the front approached in spring 1938 and fell to Nationalist troops in June 1938 during the drive towards Valencia.

levant-14.rem: The shelter tells the war as civilians lived it, in a city that changed hands in the middle of the war.
levant-14.st: Castelló was bombed by Nationalist and Italian aircraft as the front approached in spring 1938, and it fell to Nationalist troops in June 1938 during the drive towards Valencia. This public shelter under Plaza Tetuán was built in 1937–38 to protect the townspeople. Now part of the city museum, it presents the war as civilians lived it. Today the restored shelter offers exhibits, multimedia and audioguides in Spanish, Valencian, English and French.

levant-15.ev: Captain Bayo's Republican militia land at Porto Cristo in an attempt to retake Mallorca.

q.t: How did Bayo's expedition to Mallorca end?
o: The attackers re-embarked after a counter-attack
q.x: Reinforced by Italian aircraft, the defenders counter-attacked from 27 August; the Republicans re-embarked by 4 September, leaving equipment behind.

levant-15.rem: Captured militiamen and local leftists were executed; remains including two nurses were found at Son Coletes cemetery in Manacor.
levant-15.st: Mallorca sided with the coup in July 1936. On 16 August Captain Alberto Bayo landed Catalan and Valencian militia at Porto Cristo and Punta Amer, but the attackers were poorly coordinated, and the defenders, reinforced by Italian aircraft, counter-attacked until the Republicans re-embarked by 4 September. Captured militiamen and local leftists were executed; excavations at Son Coletes cemetery in Manacor found remains of milicianos and two nurses. Today the harbour and beaches have no major monument on the shore.

levant-10.ev: García Valiño's corps attacks the Sierra de Espadán heights but fails to take the main ridge.

q.t: What did the 1st Navarrese Division do on the captured 'Teta' summit?
o: Fortified it with bunkers and concrete walls
Handed it over to Italian troops
q.x: Left exposed after taking one of the two 'Tetas' on 18 July 1938, the division fortified it; both sides' works survive.

levant-10.rem: La Ràpita and Espadà anchored the Republican line, and the main ridge held despite heavy fighting.
levant-10.st: On the eastern part of the Línea XYZ, García Valiño's corps tried to break through the Sierra de Espadán and seize the heights of La Ràpita and Espadà, which anchored the Republican line. The Nationalists took one of the two 'Tetas' summits on 18 July 1938, but heavy fighting failed to take the main ridge, and the exposed 1st Navarrese Division fortified the captured hill. Today parapets, bunkers, rock-cut trenches and sniper posts from both sides survive.

levant-16.ev: Republican prisoners are held in a Francoist penal colony beside the road across Formentera.
levant-16.rem: Many prisoners died of hunger and disease here; the site is now protected, with Coromines' poem 'The Cemetery of the Living' beside it.
levant-16.st: After the war the Franco regime set up a penal colony for Republican prisoners on Formentera, beside the road from La Savina to La Mola. Some 2,133 men passed through it, and at least 58 died of hunger and disease before it closed in November 1942; they were buried in Sant Francesc cemetery, where remains have been exhumed. Today low walls, barracks foundations, wells and a plaque with Joan Coromines' poem 'The Cemetery of the Living' remain.

levant-17.ev: Work begins on a concrete shelter for about 400 people beside the Torres de Serranos.

q.t: What has become an emblem of Valencia's wartime design?
q.x: The Art Deco 'REFUGIO' lettering on Valencia's shelters has become an emblem of the city's wartime design.

levant-17.rem: This is one of more than 50 public shelters Valencia built against raids by Italian bombers based in Mallorca.
levant-17.st: Valencia built more than 50 public shelters against the raids carried out by Italian bombers based in Mallorca from 1937 to 1939. This one, very probably the shelter begun on 22 June 1937 at Calle Serranos 25, held about 400 people in three reinforced-concrete chambers under a roof more than 1.5 m thick. Its Art Deco 'REFUGIO' lettering has become an emblem of wartime Valencia. Today the three chambers keep original features, with interpretation panels.

west-01.ev: Yagüe's Army of Africa columns storm Badajoz, charging through machine-gun fire at the Puerta de la Trinidad.

q.t: Why was the fall of Badajoz strategically important?
o: It gave the Nationalists an Atlantic port
It joined the Nationalist zones of south and north
It cut Madrid off from Valencia
q.x: Badajoz's fall linked the Nationalist zones and opened the road up the Tagus valley towards Madrid.

west-01.rem: What followed inside the city became one of the war's most notorious episodes of repression.
west-01.st: On 14 August 1936 Lt-Col. Juan Yagüe's Army of Africa columns stormed Badajoz, defended by Col. Ildefonso Puigdendolas with loyal troops and militia. At the Puerta de la Trinidad the 16th Company of the Legion's 4th Bandera charged through machine-gun fire and suffered heavy losses before the walls were carried. The city's fall opened the road towards Madrid, and what followed inside became one of the war's most notorious episodes of repression. Today the 17th-century gate and walls survive.

west-02.ev: After Badajoz falls, militiamen and Popular Front supporters are rounded up, held in the bullring and shot.
west-02.rem: The memorial in the lobby recalls those killed after the city fell; how many died is still disputed.
west-02.st: After Badajoz fell, Nationalist troops and Falangists rounded up militiamen, Popular Front supporters and people found with bruised shoulders from rifle recoil. Many were held in the bullring and shot; the death toll, and whether shootings took place inside the ring itself, are disputed. Reports by Mário Neves, Jay Allen and other journalists made 'Badajoz' known worldwide. Today a congress hall stands on the site, with the 'Memorial Badajoz 1936' display in its lobby.

west-06.ev: Nationalist authorities hold thousands of Republican soldiers and civilians here awaiting classification and trial.
west-06.rem: Many held here were taken out and shot; the camp's ditch, streets and foundations survive as one of Spain's best-preserved Francoist camp layouts.
west-06.st: When the Republican Army of Extremadura surrendered at the end of March 1939, Nationalist authorities built a camp on the La Verilleja estate near Castuera. For about a year it held thousands of Republican soldiers and civilians awaiting classification and trial; many were taken out and shot, though the number executed is not established. It is one of the best-preserved Francoist camp layouts in Spain. Today the perimeter ditch, camp streets, barrack foundations and the base of the cross remain.

west-03.ev: Legion troops rush the mined Roman bridge over the Guadiana and break into Mérida.

q.t: What happened to the demolition charges on the Roman bridge?
o: They destroyed the bridge's central arches
q.x: The defenders had mined the bridge, but the charges were not fired; Nationalist accounts credit Alarcón de la Lastra with disarming them.

west-03.rem: Mérida's capture linked Seville with the northern zone; mass detentions and executions followed in the town.
west-03.st: Mérida was the key road and rail junction between the Nationalist south and north. On 10 August 1936 the Legion's 5th Bandera rushed the Roman bridge, which the defenders had mined; the charges were not fired, and the troops broke into the city, linking Seville with Mola's northern zone. Mass detentions and executions at the cemetery wall followed. Today the Roman bridge over the Guadiana is pedestrian, and a cemetery memorial remembers the victims of the repression.

west-07.ev: Italian units of the Flechas Azules brigade create a war cemetery here for their dead.

q.t: How does the Campillo de Llerena museum present the war?
o: As a place of remembrance for victims of both sides
As a celebration of the Italian units
As a display of weapons only
q.x: Extremadura's first Civil War museum explains trench life on both sides and presents itself as a place of remembrance for victims of both sides.

west-07.rem: The restored Italian cemetery and the museum form one complex on the static southern Extremadura front.
west-07.st: Campillo de Llerena lay just behind the Nationalist line on the static southern Extremadura front. In 1937 Italian units of the mixed Italo-Spanish 'Flechas Azules' brigade, based here, created a war cemetery for their dead. With the town's Civil War museum, the restored cemetery forms a complex presented as a place of remembrance for victims of both sides. Today the walled Italian cemetery lies outside the village, and the museum in town has a reconstructed trench and bunker.

west-04.ev: Militiamen barricaded in the church tower hold out for a week, then surrender and are shot.
west-04.rem: The cemetery memorial names victims of the repression that followed; earlier, right-wing prisoners had also been killed in the town.
west-04.st: On 7 August 1936 Asensio's and Castejón's columns entered Almendralejo on their drive north from Seville. About fifty militiamen barricaded themselves in the tower of the Purificación church and held out for a week before surrendering, and were then shot. The town suffered heavy repression, while earlier, under Republican control, several right-wing prisoners had also been killed; numbers on both sides are debated. Today the church tower stands on Plaza de España, and a 2023 cemetery memorial names victims.

west-05.ev: Franco directs the Army of Africa's advance towards Talavera and Toledo from this Renaissance palace.

q.t: What happened to Franco while he was based here in late September 1936?
o: He was wounded in an air raid
He signed the final war communiqué
His fellow generals chose him as commander-in-chief
q.x: Fellow generals chose him as commander-in-chief and head of the rebel state, before the formal proclamation in Burgos on 1 October.

west-05.rem: The palace shows how the rebel command was improvised in private buildings of provincial towns.
west-05.st: From 26 August 1936 Franco set up his headquarters in this Renaissance palace in Cáceres, directing the Army of Africa's advance up the Tagus towards Talavera and Toledo. In late September, while based here, he was chosen by his fellow generals as commander-in-chief and head of the rebel state. The palace shows how the rebel command was improvised in private buildings of provincial towns. Today its fine façade stands in the walled old town; a Francoist plaque has drawn removal requests.

west-08.ev: Republican engineers and local masons build machine-gun posts and zigzag trenches along the Guadámez valley.

q.t: What inscription does one of the Republican machine-gun posts carry?
q.x: One of the concrete-and-brick posts carries 'AÑO 1937'. In July 1938 Queipo de Llano's Army of the South cut off much of the pocket.

west-08.rem: Unlike the famous fronts, the works of the La Serena pocket survive almost untouched and little visited.
west-08.st: From late 1936 the Republic held a large salient in eastern Badajoz, the 'La Serena pocket'. Along the Guadámez valley Republican engineers and local masons built concrete-and-brick machine-gun posts linked by zigzag trenches, one inscribed 'AÑO 1937'. In July 1938 Queipo de Llano's Army of the South attacked, taking Castuera, Campanario and Villanueva de la Serena. Today small fortines and stretches of trench survive, almost untouched, at Cañada Honda and Los Palancares.

castile-01.ev: Franco lives and works in this mansion while Burgos serves as the political capital of Nationalist Spain.

q.t: What did Franco sign here on 1 April 1939?
o: The final war communiqué: 'the war has ended'
The decree unifying Falange and Carlists
His investiture as head of state
q.x: On 1 April 1939 Franco signed the final war communiqué here, in the mansion he used as residence and headquarters until October 1939.

castile-01.rem: Burgos was Nationalist Spain's political capital: the Junta sat here and Franco's first government was formed here in January 1938.
castile-01.st: Burgos was the political capital of Nationalist Spain: the Junta de Defensa Nacional sat here from July 1936, and Franco was invested as head of state in the city on 1 October 1936. From August 1937 until October 1939 this mansion served as his residence and headquarters, and here on 1 April 1939 he signed the final war communiqué announcing that the war had ended. Today the neo-Renaissance mansion stands in gardens on the Paseo de la Isla.

castile-03.ev: The Nationalists gather papers seized from Republican parties, unions and lodges as material for repression.

q.t: What were the 'papeles de Salamanca'?
o: Nationalist battle plans captured by the Republic
Catalan government papers returned to Catalonia from 2006

castile-03.rem: An archive built for repression now serves historians and relatives of victims of both sides.
castile-03.st: In 1937–38 the Nationalists set up a documents office in Salamanca to gather papers seized from Republican parties, unions, Masonic lodges and individuals, raw material for the repression. The archive became the Centro Documental de la Memoria Histórica in 2007 and now serves historians and relatives of victims of both sides; the return of Catalan government papers from 2006 was contested. Today a permanent exhibition includes a lodge room reconstructed from confiscated regalia, and a reading room serves researchers.

castile-04.ev: Pamplona builds a domed monument to the Nationalist dead, whose crypt later holds Mola and Sanjurjo.
castile-04.rem: Whether to reinterpret or demolish the monument remains one of Spain's liveliest debates over uncomfortable heritage.
castile-04.st: Pamplona was the base of Gen. Emilio Mola, 'the Director' of the July 1936 coup, and Navarre sent thousands of Carlist requetés to the Nationalist side, while more than 3,000 Navarrese left-wingers were killed in the rearguard. The domed Monument to the Fallen of Navarre honoured the Nationalist dead, and its crypt held Mola and Sanjurjo until 2016. Whether to reinterpret or demolish it remains contested. Today the massive building dominates Avenida Carlos III, its Francoist inscriptions covered.

castile-05.ev: Republican prisoners overpower guards and escape from the fort in the largest prison break of the war.
castile-05.rem: Few escapers reached safety; many who died here lie in the nearby 'bottle cemetery', their names once placed in bottles on the graves.
castile-05.st: This 19th-century fort on Mount Ezkaba, above Pamplona, served as a political prison where about 2,500 Republican prisoners were held in damp, overcrowded casemates. On 22 May 1938 some 795 escaped in the largest prison break of the war; hunted through the hills of Navarre, around 200 were killed, most were recaptured and only three reached France. Scores more died of disease in the fort. Today its moats and casemates remain, and nearby lies the 'bottle cemetery'.

castile-02.ev: Franco directs the attack on Madrid and the war in the North from the bishop's palace.

q.t: Who lent Franco the bishop's palace in Salamanca?
q.x: Bishop Pla y Deniel, whose 1936 pastoral framed the war as a crusade, lent the palace, making Salamanca the rebel zone's working capital.

castile-02.rem: From here Franco also oversaw the unification of Falange and Carlists in April 1937.
castile-02.st: After his investiture as head of state, Franco moved his headquarters to Salamanca, into the bishop's palace lent by Bishop Enrique Pla y Deniel, whose 1936 pastoral framed the war as a crusade. From here Franco directed the attack on Madrid, the war in the North and the unification of Falange and Carlists in April 1937, making Salamanca the rebel zone's working capital. Today the palace beside the New Cathedral houses the Museo Diocesano.

castile-06.ev: Men of Sartaguda, including the socialist mayor and councillors, are killed in the rearguard repression.
castile-06.rem: Known as 'the village of widows', Sartaguda now holds Navarre's main memorial, a wall bearing the names of victims from across the region.
castile-06.st: Navarre saw no front-line fighting, yet its rearguard repression of 1936 was severe. In the small village of Sartaguda at least 86 people were killed, including the socialist mayor and councillors, and it became known as 'the village of widows'. The Parque de la Memoria, opened in 2008, is Navarre's main memorial to the victims of Francoist repression. Today a long wall bears the names of Navarrese killed in their villages, at Ezkaba, in Mauthausen or in forced labour.

castile-07.ev: Republican prisoners, then foreigners fleeing across the Pyrenees, are held in Franco's longest-running concentration camp.
castile-07.rem: Remembered here are Republican prisoners, International Brigaders and the wartime refugees and evaders held in the camp until 1947.
castile-07.st: Opened in 1937 beside the railway junction, Miranda de Ebro was the longest-running of Franco's concentration camps, closing only in January 1947. Large numbers of Republican prisoners passed through it, including captured International Brigaders. During the Second World War it became the main internment camp for foreigners crossing the Pyrenees, with over 3,500 held at once in a camp built for 1,500. Today a few remains and a plaque stand among industrial plants, and a town interpretation centre has a reconstructed barrack.

castile-09.ev: The monastery of San Marcos becomes one of Spain's largest prison camps after León falls to the rebels.
castile-09.rem: Behind the famous façade thousands of men and women were held; survivors' associations still seek recognition of its prison past.
castile-09.st: León fell to the rebels in the first days of the war, and the vast Renaissance monastery of San Marcos became one of the largest prison camps in Spain. Men from León, Asturias and the Northern front, and women in a separate section, were crowded into its halls and stables, and many were executed or died of disease. Survivors' associations have long sought recognition of its prison past. Today the Plateresque façade, church and cloister can be seen; the hotel interior is not a memorial.

castile-11.ev: The former lazaretto on San Simón becomes a concentration camp and penal colony for political prisoners.
castile-11.rem: Overcrowding, hunger and disease killed many prisoners here; the island is now partly dedicated to their memory.
castile-11.st: Galicia fell to the coup within days in July 1936, and the rearguard repression was severe. The small island of San Simón, a former lazaretto in the Ría de Vigo, became a concentration camp and penal colony for political prisoners, first from Vigo and Pontevedra and later from across Spain. Overcrowding, hunger and disease killed many, and some inmates were taken out and shot. Today the restored island buildings form a cultural centre, where guided tours explain the camp period.

castile-08.ev: The ancient monastery becomes a concentration camp and, from 1938, the main camp for captured International Brigaders.
castile-08.rem: Former prisoners remembered hunger, beatings and forced saluting; no major memorial marks their captivity here.
castile-08.st: The ancient monastery near Burgos became a concentration camp in December 1936 and, from April 1938, the main camp for captured International Brigaders, held alongside Spanish prisoners until it closed in November 1939. Volunteers taken at Jarama, Belchite, Calaceite and Gandesa passed through, and the army psychiatrist Antonio Vallejo-Nágera carried out pseudo-scientific studies on inmates here. Former prisoners' memoirs describe hunger, beatings and forced saluting. Today a Trappist community lives in the restored monastery, with no major memorial to the prisoners.

castile-10.ev: Republican prisoners held in a former silk factory die of cold, hunger and disease.
castile-10.rem: Exhumations since 2007 have returned names to many who died here, one of the best-documented cases of prison mortality in Franco's Spain.
castile-10.st: In an old silk factory in the Valdivielso valley north of Burgos, the Franco regime ran a prison for Republican prisoners, many transferred from other jails and from the Northern front. Cold, hunger and disease killed 153 inmates between 1938 and 1943, and they were buried in the village cemetery; from 2007 the victims' association exhumed 114 bodies and identified many of them. Today the shell of the factory-prison stands beside the Ebro, and the cemetery holds a memorial to the prisoners.

castile-13.ev: People killed in the rearguard repression in La Rioja are buried here in three mass graves.
castile-13.rem: Relatives turned this execution and burial site into a memorial cemetery, the main place of remembrance for victims of repression in La Rioja.
castile-13.st: La Rioja fell to the rebels without a fight in July 1936, yet around two thousand people were killed in the rearguard repression of the following months. La Barranca, near Logroño, was one of the main execution and burial sites: the official heritage declaration records 407 people buried here in three mass graves, killed between 10 September and 15 December 1936. The relatives' association turned it into a memorial cemetery. Today small walls enclose name plaques and flowers left by relatives.

castile-12.ev: General Walter's 35th Division attacks across the Guadarrama towards Segovia to relieve pressure on Bilbao.

q.t: Why did the Republic launch the La Granja offensive?
o: To capture the royal palace for the government
To link up with Republican forces in Asturias
q.x: The attack from the Navacerrada pass aimed to relieve pressure on Bilbao; initial gains were lost and it was called off within a week.

castile-12.rem: Hemingway set 'For Whom the Bell Tolls' against the preparations for this attack.
castile-12.st: To relieve pressure on Bilbao, the Republic attacked across the Sierra de Guadarrama towards Segovia. On 30 May 1937 General Walter's 35th Division, including the XIV International Brigade, struck from the Navacerrada pass against Nationalist positions above La Granja, but initial gains were lost to counter-attacks and Condor Legion air strikes, and the offensive was called off within a week. Hemingway set 'For Whom the Bell Tolls' against its preparations. Today scattered trenches remain in the pine forest above La Granja.
